entries.title: Tre Jones playing every angle for Bulls, frustrating one big at a time
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — A smirk came across Tre Jones’ face when asked if there’s a time when he knows he’s got a guy.</p><p>That split second where the team’s opposing shot blocker thinks he’s about to make the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls’</a> 6-foot-1 guard another victim only to quickly realize it’s instead going to be an “Oh (bleep)” moment for him.</p><p>Several Timberwolves players went through that at the start of this three-city road trip, including Rudy Gobert, and then in Cleveland Jones got 6-9 Thomas Jones twice.</p><p>Not only are there few Bulls players on the roster that are as quick as Jones, but even fewer that understand angles at the rim.</p><p>“He’s incredibly smart at attacking those angles; super-fast too,” coach Tiago Splitter said of his reserve point guard. “Finishing at the rim, reverses, you name it, all kinds of finishes. And also taking care of the ball. I think he’s been superb so far this season taking care of the ball and finding teammates.”</p><p>He has, but that’s not what frustrates opposing players. It’s Jones’ ability to use the rim or their own body against them, angling his body for baskets players his size aren’t supposed to get.</p><p>“I’d say it was always a strength of mine growing up but continuing to try and perfect it as I get older and older in this league,” Jones said of his rare skillset. “You see the different opportunities, different defenses, and just the difference of the professional game and college where college had a lot more guys in the paint, a lot more clogged, tougher to get all the way to the hoop.</p><p>“Here in the league guys can’t just camp out in the lane. There’s a different gravity that players generate because some guys can really score the ball, so using that to my advantage as well. When the rim is taken away, I’m able to make the right play and spray it out to those guys.”</p><p>As for that moment in a game when Jones knows a big is about to misread the situation and think he’s going to block him?</p><p>“Yeah, usually there’s a split second where I feel like I might have him in a tough spot where I don’t think he can recover,” he said with a smile. “So yeah, I usually have a pretty good idea.”</p><p></p><h3>Josh-ing around</h3><p></p><p>Fresh off a six-turnover game in Cleveland, Josh Giddey spent some time with Splitter watching film and trying to correct the ball security issue.</p><p>A problem the point guard wasn’t even trying to hide from. </p><p>“Sloppy with the ball against an active team, and it was on me,” Giddey said after that loss to the Cavs. “It was just bad from the start all around. Turnovers, defense, everything. I just want to put it in the trash and move on.”</p><p>Splitter came out of the film session feeling better.</p><p>“Just trying to help him try and see what’s going on in his mind, what he sees,” Splitter said. “The end of the day we’ve got to be more careful with the ball. Sometimes just play simple and make the easy pass, but I think he’s going to get better, bounce back.”</p><p>Maybe, but he did have two turnovers in the first five minutes against Brooklyn on Wednesday.</p><p></p><h3>Rising stock</h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>Two-way contract guard Jaylin Sellers was named G League Player of the Week after averaging 26.6 points per game. Expect the Providence standout to move into the big-boy rotation at some point later this year. Splitter sure does.</p><p>“Helluva defender, he can shoot, he can be aggressive at the rim,” Splitter said of Sellers. “He’s doing what we’ve seen in the gym all summer. I love that kid. He’s going to be a part of our future for sure.”</p>

entries.title: Grant Taylor excited to join White Sox rotation that should see another addition
entries.summary: <p>With the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> shifting flamethrower Grant Taylor from relief ace to starting pitcher, it’s almost mandatory to draw parallels to a similar effort with Chris Sale 15 years prior.</p><p>After throwing 192 innings of 3.05 ERA-ball and making the first of what are now 10 All-Star appearances in what will almost certainly be a Hall of Fame career, Sale’s 2012 season is the archetype reliever conversion; both in terms of results and casting aside injury fears that once dogged his unusual delivery.</p><p>Yet, the Sox process with the 24-year-old Taylor will differ in some notable, ideally beneficial ways.</p><p>While arguing for his spot in the rotation with then-general manager Ken Williams eventually became part of Sale’s legend, Taylor touts a frictionless process where he made his wishes to start well-known, fulfilled the organization’s aims for a transition year in relief, and had an amiable conversation with GM Chris Getz confirming his role for 2027.</p><p>“They were all on board,” Taylor said Wednesday. “I want to help my team win and I think the game reflects that throwing more innings and doing it well helps your team win more often.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Grant Taylor innings are good, so more Grant Taylor innings should be more good. It's science. <a href="https://t.co/JXMYUUZ1Z7">pic.twitter.com/JXMYUUZ1Z7</a></p>— James Fegan (@JRFegan) <a href="https://x.com/JRFegan/status/2123209971315749040?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 19, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Pitching alongside Jake Peavy’s last elite season and Jose Quintana’s breakout campaign, Sale powered a formidable trio in the first half of 2012. But when he (4.03 ERA after the All-Star break) and Quintana understandably ran out of gas late, the Sox’ lacking depth was exposed in a September collapse that handed the division title to Detroit.</p><p>After a 2026 postseason pitching plan that relied heavily on Taylor, Sean Burke, and off days, the Sox are hoping to build a deeper group. A source indicated to the Sun-Times the front office is looking to follow up this week’s agreement with Dustin May with another rotation addition of similar magnitude.</p><p>“A lot of guys are pumped up to get a guy like that,” Chase Meidroth said of May. “Facing him when he was with the Dodgers, my first year, he was unbelievable. He’s one of those arms you are happy he’s on your team.”</p><p>With Davis Martin, Noah Schultz, David Sandlin and others also gunning for rotation spots, the Sox hope to have the flexibility to rest Taylor as needed. And after battling injuries as a prospect, Taylor hopes to not require any breathers.</p><p>“Over the past few years I've built a pretty good team behind me,” Taylor said of his personal training staff. “I'm going to be relying on them a little bit more this year than I would in a typical offseason.”</p><h3>New assistant hitting coach</h3><p>Sources tell the Sun-Times the White Sox will hire Rays hitting coordinator Kyle Wilson to be their assistant hitting coach. Wilson will replace Joel McKeithan, who departed to become the Cardinals lead hitting coach.</p><h3>Leasure DFA’d</h3><p>With the signing of May becoming official, the Sox designated reliever Jordan Leasure for assignment to make room on the 40-man roster. Leasure will miss the 2027 season recovering from elbow surgery.</p>

entries.title: Picking the favorites in 11 of the area's top high school basketball conferences
entries.summary: <p>Whether it’s the preseason rankings or a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-basketball-rankings/2026/11/17/michael-obriens-preseason-super-25-illinois-high-school-basketball-rankings" >Super 25</a> appearance at some point this winter, all of these conference favorites should be in the rankings conversation over the next several months.</p><p>Here are the favorites in many of the top conferences around the Chicago area.</p><p><b>Catholic League Blue: Benet</b></p><p>With the Catholic League adding East Suburban Catholic Conference schools this year — hello Class 4A state finalists Marist and Benet — this is without question the strongest league in the state. And it’s not close.</p><p>This Benet team isn’t returning quite the nucleus it has over the past couple of years. Inexperienced players will have to prove themselves. But it’s a team with the state’s top senior prospect in 6-8 Ed Stasys, along with 6-4 senior Perry Tchiegne and a host of talented newcomers.</p><p><b>Central Suburban League North: Niles North and Deerfield</b></p><p>A fun two-team race without a true favorite featuring a pair of teams led by the league’s best players: Deerfield’s Tommy Donahue and Niles North’s Colin Tobin.</p><p><b>Central Suburban League South: Evanston</b></p><p>As always, the CSL South will be strong again. But the defending league champs have four returning starters back as Vito Rocca, Tate Schroeder, Ben Ojala and Dion Lane were all double-figure scorers last season.</p><p><b>DuKane Conference: Glenbard North</b></p><p>On paper, Glenbard North is a prohibitive favorite with the Big Two of 6-3 Lamari Carpenter and 6-5 Oturo Redento. This pair combined to average 29 points, 10 rebounds and six assists a game last season as juniors. They are two of four returning starters from a conference and regional championship team.</p><p><b>DuPage Valley Conference: Neuqua Valley</b></p><p>With everyone back, including the most potent 1-2 scoring punch in the state in junior star Cole Kelly and Illinois recruit Mason Martin, Neuqua is head and shoulders above the rest of the pack.</p><p><b>Mid-Suburban League: Buffalo Grove</b></p><p>What is clearly the top team in the MSL, Buffalo Grove, led by 6-9 Alex Sirbu, isn’t playing in the MSL’s top division. The Bison should run through the MSL East and be favored to win the MSL title game.</p><p><b>North Suburban Conference: Warren</b></p><p>Yes, Jaxson Davis has departed — as did four other key players. But the slight edge still goes to the Blue Devils over contenders like Stevenson, Libertyville and Lake Forest.</p><p><b>Southland: Bloom </b></p><p>This will be a dogfight and fun conference race to watch all winter between Thornwood, Rich and the young, up-and-coming Bloom team that has added Thornwood transfer Lester Watson (14 ppg). Bloom gets the slight edge with the backcourt of Watson and sophomores Keiwon Gulley and Kaden McClellan.</p><p><b>Southwest Prairie West: Bolingbrook</b></p><p>Oswego will be ranked. Yorkville has its top players back from a regional title team. But Bolingbrook, led by star Brady Pettigrew, is loaded with too much talent, led by star Brady Pettigrew.</p><p><b>Southwest Suburban: Homewood-Flossmoor and Lockport</b></p><p>Take your pick between two equal favorites.</p><p>Lockport is ready to pounce as four starters return from a 27-win team. But until H-F is knocked off its perch — the Vikings have won three straight conference championships while going 38-2 the past three years in league play — you can’t discount coach Brandin Brown’s team as the one to beat.</p><p>There would be no surprise if H-F and the Porters split the regular season meetings and shared a conference championship.</p><p><b>West Suburban Silver: Lyons</b></p><p>Lyons and York shared the Silver title last year and will battle it out again, while Downers Grove North will be pesky all winter long. But the return of 6-5 Grant Smith and 6-4 point guard Timmy Sloan gives LT the edge.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-430000" name="html-embed-module-430000"></a><iframe title="No Shot Clock, Ep. 207: Revealing the 2026-27 statewide preseason Super 25 rankings" allowtransparency="true" height="150" width="100%" style="border: none; min-width: min(100%, 430px);height:150px;" scrolling="no" data-name="pb-iframe-player" src="https://www.podbean.com/player-v2/?i=u6iwm-1bb41bc-pb&from=pb6admin&share=1&download=1&rtl=0&fonts=Arial&skin=1&font-color=auto&logo_link=episode_page&btn-skin=c73a3a" loading="lazy"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Bulls dominate the Nets in a Brooklyn homecoming for coach and player
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK – With 8:55 left in the opening quarter, a baby-faced, then-20-year-old Nic Claxton appeared on the massive video screen hanging center court at the Barclays Center.</p><p>A tribute to the seven years he put in as a Net, with highlights of the 6-foot-11 center first being selected out of Georgia and looking every bit a wide-eyed rookie, to some of his better in-game highlights through the years.</p><p>Claxton looked up from the Bulls bench, watching intently, and when it ended raised his hand up to the crowd to let him know that it really meant something to him.</p><p>A nice moment in his homecoming on Wednesday.</p><p>Not the only feel-good moment for the visiting Bulls, either.</p><p>Finishing off a three-city road trip that started with a massive shocker in Minnesota when they upset the Timberwolves, the Bulls (4-10) continued looking like a group that was starting to get the vision that coach Tiago Splitter has been patiently trying to instill, dominating Brooklyn 137-107.</p><p>It helps when the offense can continue to find its range from three-point land (21-of-45 for the game) and the defense isn’t allowing a lay-up line, but it’s also a group that seems to have a better feel for their roles, both with the starting group and the reserves.</p><p>Which Splitter has been harping on since the season tipped off in embarrassing fashion in Toronto.</p><p>The win against the Nets, however, was important for several reasons, with the first being Claxton wasn’t the only homecoming on Wednesday.</p><p>The Barclays Center was where Splitter got his first chance at NBA coaching, hired by the Nets as an assistant in 2019.</p><p>“Great things happened here, a lot of friends, learned a lot at the beginning of a coaching career,” Splitter said. “New York, a lot of good players, then rebuilding; we went through a lot of stages together. Grateful for that time here.”</p><p>And grateful for the lessons it taught him, as Splitter weathered a 1-9 start to this season, sitting in the Bulls coaching seat for the first time. A streak that could have wilted his confidence a bit if he hadn’t seen it in his days when the Nets were in rebuild mode.</p><p>“It’s kind of like a little bit of what Taj has going on right now,” Splitter said, referring to what former Bulls veteran Taj Gibson was experiencing now that he’s gone from player to first-year assistant coach. “You were a former player, you come in, you’re part of these coaches’ meetings and you see what’s going on behind the scenes a little bit, and just how to put everything together.</p><p>“It was a learning process. And I remember Nic also, trying to figure out the league, his first steps here, and how much he has grown since then. It’s rewarding to see guys getting better.”</p><p>That’s because Claxton was with Splitter in those rough days. Years later, different team, and the two are again trying to right the ship.</p><p>Made easier on nights like this when the Bulls were out to show that they are by no means a playoff team or even a play-in team, but they aren’t the worst team in the NBA, either.</p><p>Baby steps.</p><p>Thanks to a 37-point first quarter in which the Bulls hit 8-of-18 from three behind 16 combined points from Norman Powell and Josh Giddey, the visiting team never looked back, leading by as much as 37 at one point.</p><p>Matas Buzelis led the Bulls with 25 points – the first time this season he’s put together 20-plus-point games back-to-back.</p><p>“It’s a credit to this team,” Buzelis said of the 2-1 road trip. “We’re playing great basketball and at the end of the day that’s all that matters.</p><p>“We knew how to attack (the Nets), and every game is different. This game it was finding the pocket, getting the one extra (pass) … it’s all scouting report and how we’re going to attack.”</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Concerns grow over aging hoarder sister
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My immediate family consists only of my brother (75, same age as me) and a sister who's four years older than us. My sister, "Marilyn," is divorced with no children. She has a long-term diagnosis of depression and remains under the care of a psychiatrist, who has her on several medications.</p><p>Marilyn has a shopping addiction and an issue with money. She purchased a condominium for some $20,000 in the 1970s. Now she owes about $80,000 on it. Whenever she needed money for a large purchase, such as a car, she took out another mortgage, dipping into its equity. She loves jewelry and has piles of it all over her home. Her income is $80,000 per year, but she's been through bankruptcy for debts and a foreclosure for failure to pay condo fees. We've tried for years to get her rein in her spending.</p><p>Marilyn is in failing health, and her home is a hoarder nightmare, requiring one to climb over items just to get to the bathroom. Should she need assisted living or a nursing home, she has no ability to pay for it. My brother and I are adamant that we won't assist her financially, but we worry. Marilyn won't help us by signing a financial power of attorney, a will or a transfer-on-death deed for her condo. She has managed to maintain herself, albeit chaotically and on the edge, so guardianship would not be appropriate. I have no wish to be her guardian anyway. What advice do you have about this situation? — <i>BELEAGUERED BROTHER</i></p><p><b>DEAR BROTHER:</b> You can't force Marylin to stop shopping or spending money she doesn't have, but you can help ensure that she's not a physical danger to herself. Because she is already under the care of a psychiatrist, it's time to inform that caregiver about Marilyn's hoarding and her shopping addiction. You can bet Marilyn hasn't brought them up! Be aware that the doctor's office won't inform you of her progress and may not even confirm that she is a patient, but they should at least listen to your concerns.</p><p>The state of her condo sounds like it poses a health risk, so a call to Adult Protective Services is in order. They can come to her home, assess the risk and put her in contact with someone who can help her get it under control.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> We gave our good friends a gift and a card for their special anniversary. When our anniversary arrived a few months later, all they gave us was a card. I know they can afford a gift, so why didn't they reciprocate? I thought we were good friends. We are feeling hurt, though we know we should get over it. Can you offer some advice? — <i>GOLDEN COUPLE IN MAINE</i></p><p><b>DEAR GOLDEN COUPLE:</b> Your friends appear to be less invested (literally and figuratively) in anniversaries than you are. Friendships should not be measured by whether gifts are exchanged. Perhaps your friends were trying to tell you it's time to cut back on the gift-giving at this point in your lives. Whatever the reason, don't let this spoil a meaningful friendship.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: In prison for child porn, ex-Chicagoan argues sentence unfairly limits his ability to raise 'future children'
entries.summary: <p>Convicted last year on child pornography charges, imprisoned former Chicagoan Dovid Akiva Shenkman argued in a recently rejected appeal that his sentence was “unreasonable” in part because it gave “probation officers too much discretion to determine whether he could associate with his future children” once he’s released from custody.</p><p>Beyond a prison sentence of 95 months and other penalties, U.S. District Judge Matthew Leitman imposed a number of “special conditions” on Shenkman once he is out of prison and subject to 10 years of “supervised release.”</p><p>“You must not have direct contact with any child you know or reasonably should know to be under the age of 18, including your own children, without the permission of the probation officer,” according to one of the conditions.</p><p>“If you do have any direct contact with any child you know or reasonably should know to be under the age of 18, including your own children, without the permission of the probation officer, you must report this contact to the probation officer within 24 hours.”</p><p>“You must not provide care or live in a residence where children under the age of eighteen (18) reside, without prior approval of the probation officer.”</p><p>In appellate documents filed since the 2025 sentencing, Shenkman’s attorneys argued that Leitman “ordered that Mr. Shenkman have no contact with his own children, but provided no explanation for that decision.”</p><p>“In doing so, it unjustifiably interfered with his fundamental rights to family association and to raise his children.”</p><p>“Notably, these conditions also provide a probation officer with unfettered discretion to determine if Mr. Shenkman could have contact with his own children” without “any safeguard or objective criteria to guide a probation officer.”</p><p>Prosecutors countered: “As for the challenged special condition of supervised release, viewing the record as a whole, the court provided more than enough justification for imposing it.”</p><p>“The condition served the twin goals of supervision — rehabilitation of the defendant and protection of the public. Prohibiting Shenkman from having direct contact with any child or living with any child, including his own children, without the permission of his probation officer, is tied directly to his personal history and characteristics, the nature and circumstances of the offense, and the need to protect the public.”</p><p>In denying Shenkman’s request that his sentence be tossed and revisited because it was “procedurally and substantively unreasonable,” the U.S. Court of Appeals wrote this month:</p><p>“Although it was the defense’s theory, supported by a doctor’s report, that Shenkman only looked at child pornography to feel something, it is obvious why the district court would restrict Shenkman’s association with minors — he possessed particularly disturbing [child sexual abuse materials] and claimed to have sexually abused children.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b80000" "A lot of times they want to get married and have children to make more victims."</p><p>Shenkman's lawyer couldn't be reached.</p><p>Shenkman, 41, made a number of other legal arguments in seeking a new sentence. Among them, that Leitman “did not address his mitigation arguments,” including that Shenkman was raised in a “dysfunctional household.”</p><p>But the appeals court indicated none of that should change what Leitman imposed.</p><p>Shenkman is being held at a prison in New Jersey. He lived in Chicago when younger and later moved to the East Coast. He was arrested in 2024 crossing from Canada into Detroit, where federal agents searched his cell phones and found exchanges of child porn via Telegram, an encrypted social media application.</p><p>Shenkman was prosecuted in Michigan, and the investigation found hundreds of videos, some depicting “the rape of infants and toddlers.”</p><p>Before he was sentenced, several Jewish religious figures in the Chicago area sent letters to the court to seek leniency, with some appearing to minimize his misconduct.</p><p>Among them: Rabbi Moshe Yosef Unger, a North Side resident who in suburban Oak Park.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Even as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/09/14/new-report-finds-35-of-chicago-households-dont-have-sufficient-food" target="_blank" ><u>food insecurity persists</u></a>, the number of people receiving food assistance in Illinois continues to decrease months after the state predicted many would lose access due to expanded work rules imposed by H.R.1, more commonly known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” championed by President Donald Trump.</p><p>By September, SNAP enrollment continued to decrease in Illinois to 1.4 million people, the lowest program participation since 2009. That amounts to about a 23% decrease in the number of people getting food assistance compared to last fall. And the future of the program remains uncertain.</p><p>Galvanized by Democrats gaining the majority in Congress, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker issued a list of <a class="Link" href="https://gov-pritzker-newsroom.prezly.com/gov-pritzker-releases-fighting-for-illinois-day-one-agenda" target="_blank" ><u>policy recommendations</u></a> for federal lawmakers. Repealing SNAP eligibility restrictions and changing the state’s financial burden to administer the program were among Pritzker’s top policy recommendations. At the same time, the Trump administration is proposing another change to SNAP that could further shrink eligibility, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/snap-eligibility-food-stamps-trump.html" target="_blank" ><u>New York Times reported</u></a>.</p><p>In Cook County, advocates are working to pinpoint what exactly is driving the enrollment decrease. Beyond adults expected to meet the expanded work requirements, participation in Cook County has also fallen among children and those 60 years and older compared from this summer to the fall, according to data from the state.</p><p>Yet, residents are still seeking out the program. In fact, the state received the most SNAP applications from Cook County residents in August and September compared to monthly data from the past two years, according to data from the Illinois Department of Human Services.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-5f0000" name="html-embed-module-5f0000"></a><div style="min-height:550px" id="datawrapper-vis-Vn7mz"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Vn7mz/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-Vn7mz"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Vn7mz/full.png" alt="Age groups for SNAP recipients in Cook County (Pie Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-240000" name="html-embed-module-240000"></a><div style="min-height:419px" id="datawrapper-vis-RzcVT"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/RzcVT/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-RzcVT"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/RzcVT/full.png" alt="SNAP applications in Cook County by month (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Margarita Muñoz, 56, of Cicero, was among those who applied for SNAP this year. She started receiving benefits in August but it was terminated by the next month for reasons she says are unclear.</p><p>Muñoz found the online application intimidating, but after completing a recent internship with Hunger Free America, she applied and got back on SNAP. She and her son, a sophomore at DePaul University, receive $25 a month in food assistance.</p><p>“Well, $25 is better than nothing,” Muñoz said.</p><p><b>Confusion leads to terminations</b><br>Earlier this year, Gwynne Kizer Mashon, associate director for the public benefits practice at Legal Aid Chicago, said lawyers got wind that a group of SNAP recipients living in a senior building planned to pull themselves voluntarily from the program because of the H.R. 1 rules. The group, which provides free legal aid, sent a paralegal to reassure the seniors living there that they could keep their benefits.</p><p>“We knew by the definition of them living there, they were exempt,” Kizer Mashon said, referencing the type of building where the seniors lived. “...They were going to proactively stop their SNAP benefits because they were so scared that if they kept their SNAP, that it would interfere with their social security benefits.”</p><p>It’s that type of confusion that could be driving some of the decline in enrollment, Kizer Mashon and other advocates said.</p><p>Congress last year expanded work rules to include 55- to 64-year-olds, veterans and parents whose youngest child is 14 years or older — a change from 18 and older. Individuals have to prove they work or volunteer 80 hours per month to continue getting benefits, but the state has implemented exemptions that would allow people to continue getting food assistance.</p><p>Some exemptions include earning at least $935 per month in gross income, experiencing chronic homelessness or being the main caretaker for an incapacitated or disabled said they’ve been successful in all but a handful of cases involving people seeking to regain food assistance after they’ve lost it. Legal Aid Chicago has trained pro bono attorneys in Chicago who are also helping people retain their benefits.</p><p>“Most of them qualify for an exemption under Illinois rules, and either they didn’t know that they needed to submit the exemption forms or they submitted them but they got lost or something happened. We don’t know but they weren’t processed,” she said.</p><p>Another source of confusion stems from Illinois SNAP recipients who now have to prove their eligibility every six months instead of once a year, Kizer Mashon said. The notices from the state have caused confusion especially if the person just regained their benefits but remains on the same schedule to prove their eligibility, she said.</p><p>That’s led to instances in which a person gets back on SNAP only to lose it because they were confused about their redetermination date, especially since that process now requires more documentation than before H.R. 1.</p><p>“We think that there are a lot of people who are actually getting back on and then they are losing [SNAP] again because of this end of the certification period,” Kizer Mashon said. “And then they don’t understand what happened so then they just stop. That’s our experience generally with our client community is when things get too confusing, they just stop because they don’t know what else to do.”</p><p>Some additional paperwork includes providing proof of a person’s rent and shelter expenses, which is used to calculate how much in food assistance a household receives, said Autumn Clark, senior manager of public benefits partnerships with the Greater Chicago Food Depository.</p><p>Apart from H.R. 1, advocates say a new federal rule is also causing confusion among potential SNAP enrollees. The Public Charge rule, which went into effect Sept. 18, allows federal immigration officials to deny someone permanent lawful status if they believe the person is likely going to rely on government assistance programs like SNAP.</p><p>Fred Tsao, senior policy counsel at the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, said the rule applies to a small group of people, namely, those who already have green cards and don’t plan on traveling outside the country, or refugees who’ve been granted asylum.</p><p>Tsao said since the rule took effect two months ago, it’s still too early to tell how large of a deterrent effect it’ll have on potential enrollees. But what is clear, he said, is that this most recent iteration of a rule that has been around for over 140 years, is much more confusing.</p><p>“People are worried,” Tsao said. “They don't know if they are going to apply for SNAP benefits even for a U.S. citizen, spouse,or child. that people are trying to get food assistance. In August, the state received 40,739 applications for SNAP from Cook County alone, according to the Illinois Department of Human Services. In contrast, the state had received 30,308 applications in August 2025 from Cook County.</p><p>As of September, the state had approved about 166,000 applications from Cook County, compared to the nearly 255,000 applications it approved for all of 2025, according to IDHS. But as of September, the state had also denied about 78,000 applications. The state denied nearly 107,000 applications from the county for all of last year.</p><p>The Greater Chicago Food Depository is among the groups trying to curb the loss of SNAP. In November, the depository added 16 public benefits partners, like Ayala, who help community members keep SNAP benefits. In total, there’s now 40 partners doing this type of work, according to the depository.</p><p>Wanda Taylor, a benefits enrollment specialist at the Greater Chicago Food Depository, jokes that she’s known as the “bag lady” because she travels to community events with paper applications along with her laptop.</p><p>If someone has all their documentation, applying for SNAP could take less than an hour. But the process could take as long as two weeks for those who need time to get their paperwork together because the application adds up to being about 20 pages, she said.</p><p>“People are just really frustrated, confused about those job requirements,” Taylor said. “Do they want to do this for the small amount they may or may not get? … That’s a lot of what I’m hearing.”</p><p>In Springfield, Tsao’s organization is part of a coalition that lobbied to expand a state program that offers food assistance to certain immigrant victims of crime who are seeking asylum or a visa. Pritzker had proposed a $15 million cut to the Victims of Trafficking, Torture, or Other Serious Crimes program.</p><p>And while lawmakers ended up preserving the VTTC program, advocates say the state needs to go further to expand eligibility for lawfully present immigrants, including refugees and their family members, who lost SNAP access this year.</p><p>State Rep. Anna Moeller, D-Elgin, co-sponsored a bill to expand VTTC eligibility during this past spring session, which ended up languishing in House committees. Moeller, who also chairs a Health and Human Services committee, did not commit to bringing the bill back during the fall veto session this month.</p><p>But, she said, everything is on the table.</p><p>“We're also looking at supporting our food pantries and other ways that people can access food because we know that there are going to be a lot of people who are going to need it,” entries.title: A new recording unearths what may be Louis Armstrong’s most underrated performance — at Highland Park High
entries.summary: <p>As of this week, Louis Armstrong’s music has traveled further than anything else in human history.</p><p>On Wednesday morning, the interstellar probe Voyager 1 reached one light-day away from Earth, or the distance it takes light to travel in one day. On board is a golden record containing sights and sounds from our humble planet. Among them: a 1927 recording of Armstrong, playing with the Hot Seven band he founded in Chicago.</p><p>But Armstrong left us plenty of surprises here on Earth. Last week, Verve Records released <a class="Link" href="https://store.ververecords.com/products/louis-armstrong-one-night-in-highland-park-live-blizzard-lp?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24430075125&gbraid=0AAAAApCfPvNO5uAnIEAr1vrRNP8eeHLbu&gclid=Cj0KCQiAwdDXBhDuARIsAFdLukl9Bll_Bv_vzo_-K95ZWy8D-GNt3HseSq-B_SEUdbGhrgIl18SsvpIaAp36EALw_wcB" target="_blank" ><u>a never-before-heard bootleg </u></a>of the iconic trumpeter and singer performing with his All Stars Band at — of all places — a high school auditorium in Highland Park. </p><p>The concert was a fundraiser for a local synagogue, which was renamed B’nai Torah shortly after the concert. It closed permanently in 2014.</p><p>The Highland Park concert would not survive — much less in such a high-quality recording — were it not for Joel Goldstein, an 87-year-old resident of Laguna Woods, Calif., who provided the tape to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.louisarmstronghouse.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Louis Armstrong House Museum</u></a> in Queens, New York. At the time of the recording, Goldstein was a 17-year-old student stage manager at Highland Park High School, where a 1,200-seat auditorium hosted the benefit concert.</p><p>Goldstein and his friend Ron Johnson, another student in charge of audio, decided to record the concert using the auditorium’s state-of-the-art sound equipment. After all, it wasn’t every day Louis Armstrong came to your high school.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0a6426e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1529x858+0+85/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2F4d%2F048c82764139b396ba4bbe2e8577%2Fjoel-and-ron-on-his-chevrolet-biscayne-july-4-1957.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Joel Goldstein (left) and his classmate Ron Johnson, pictured here on July 4, 1957, were students in charge of audio during a Louis Armstrong concert that spring at Highland Park High. Goldstein decided to record the concert using the auditorium’s state-of-the-art sound equipment and kept the bootleg for decades. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Joel Goldstein</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“I don't think anybody besides myself and my immediate family had any awareness that we had done this, because I didn't want to go to jail,” Goldstein remembers, with a chuckle.</p><p>After graduating from Highland Park High School, Goldstein briefly attended Purdue University before transferring to Grinnell College, in Iowa. There, he was classmates with jazz icon and fellow Chicagoan <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/04/28/herbie-hancock-international-jazz-day-chicago-history-music-lyric-opera" target="_blank" ><u>Herbie Hancock</u></a>, who lived in the same residence hall.</p><p>“Everybody knew he was gifted,” Goldstein says of Hancock, who would, just a few short years after college, become the pianist in Miles Davis’s legendary Second Great Quintet.</p><p>Decades later, when Goldstein contacted the Louis Armstrong House Museum and told research director Ricky Riccardi about the recording, Riccardi wasn’t all that shocked. Armstrong and his All Stars band frequently tacked community appearances to their tours, and this cause would have been important to him: Armstrong expressed a “long time admiration for the Jewish people,” owing to close friendships with a neighboring family in New Orleans and his manager, Joe Glaser. He wore at least two different Star of David pendants around his neck throughout his life. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-430000" name="image-430000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b18f1f5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2300x1291+0+112/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F82%2Fb7f995f84f4c911b749480af38be%2Fgettyimages-1182539631-jpeg.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0a08e6c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2300x1291+0+112/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F82%2Fb7f995f84f4c911b749480af38be%2Fgettyimages-1182539631-jpeg.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e839f69/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2300x1291+0+112/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F82%2Fb7f995f84f4c911b749480af38be%2Fgettyimages-1182539631-jpeg.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="American jazzman Louis Armstrong blows his trumpet in a black and white photo taken in Paris. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e839f69/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2300x1291+0+112/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F82%2Fb7f995f84f4c911b749480af38be%2Fgettyimages-1182539631-jpeg.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7bd917e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2300x1291+0+112/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F82%2Fb7f995f84f4c911b749480af38be%2Fgettyimages-1182539631-jpeg.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e839f69/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2300x1291+0+112/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F78%2F82%2Fb7f995f84f4c911b749480af38be%2Fgettyimages-1182539631-jpeg.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>American jazzman Louis Armstrong performs during a concert in Paris on June 5, 1965.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by AFP via Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>What Riccardi <i>didn’t</i> expect was how exceptionally well-recorded the tape was, capturing an All Stars lineup that was “on fire”: trombonist Trummy Young, clarinetist Edmond Hall, pianist Billy Kyle, bassist Squire Gersh and drummer Barrett Deems, a Chicago fixture whose kit is still on display at Andy’s Jazz Club in River North. (Riccardi hails him as a “proto-punk rock drummer.”)</p><p>“This is the most exciting band I've ever heard,” Riccardi says. “And, you know, this is not Carnegie Hall; this is not the Newport Jazz Festival. It's just a stop in Highland Park on the way to the next one, [but they’re] still playing with that fire and energy.”</p><p>Armstrong’s own small-format band, the All Stars, marked a return to the combos of the trumpeter's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/10/21/23411007/louis-armstrong-jazz-history-chicago" >influential early career</a> in Chicago. The bands he played in here from 1922 to 1929 — King Oliver’s Creole Jazz Band, then his own Hot Five and Hot Seven — hugely influenced the development of early jazz.</p><p>By his All Stars era, however, critics felt Armstrong was a shadow of the pioneering trumpeter and bandleader he once was. Nor was the criticism purely musical. Activists were disappointed that Armstrong didn’t use his massive platform to speak out more forcefully about civil rights.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Armstrong, right, autographs a group picture made in the Blue Note nightclub during a jazz concert for teenagers in Chicago on April 1, 1948. Standing at left is Paul Meyer, 16, and at center is Tom Koch, 17, of Milwaukee, Wis., who hitch-hiked to Chicago to attend the afternoon concert. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by Edward S. Kitch/AP Photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The 1957 All Stars tour — the very sweep that included the Highland Park concert — marked a turning point. School desegregation in Little Rock, Ark., dominated the headlines, as did the fierce opposition by white residents and local authorities. The integrated All Stars faced their own vitriol on the road: Playing in Knoxville, Tenn., a month before the Highland Park concert, the group was mid-concert when the building trembled. The city’s White Citizens Council had lobbed dynamite at the venue from a moving car.</p><p>By the time he and the All Stars arrived in Fargo, N.D. in September — playing yet another school auditorium concert — Armstrong had reached his breaking point. He spoke candidly to a student journalist about the crisis in Little Rock, calling President Dwight D. Eisenhower “two-faced” and Arkansas governor Orval Faubus a name so vulgar it couldn’t be printed. (Armstrong and the journalist mutually settled on “uneducated plow boy” as a euphemism.)</p><p>Most consequently, Armstrong threatened to withdraw from a planned tour of the Soviet Union, one of several orchestrated by the State Department as a propaganda initiative during the Cold War. “The way they are treating my people in the South, the government can go to hell,” Armstrong said.</p><p>Riccardi feels Armstrong was just as underestimated musically during this period. His playing is nimble and energetic across the concert, which is full of All Stars signatures. The band opens its sets as it usually would, with the one-two punch of “When It’s Sleepy Time Down South” and “Indiana,” and closes with a swinging rendition of “When the Saints Go Marching In.” At the very end, Armstrong asks the audience to stand for “The Star-Spangled Banner,” a tribute to the country he loved enough to criticize.</p><p>“They're saying that he’s coasting and he's phoning it in,” Riccardi says. “If you think he was coasting, this concert will dispel all of that.”</p><p>As for the surreptitious recorder, Goldstein went on to work for federal agencies in Washington, D.C., like the National Institute of Mental Health and Substance Abuse and Mental Services Administration. After retiring, he and his wife moved to California in 2010. He carted around the audio all that time — first the original tape, then a copy he digitized in the 1980s.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> By then, Johnson, the former audio manager, had passed away, and Goldstein wondered if the museum could benefit from a copy of the tape. He was shocked when Riccardi responded to his offer a week later, suggesting that the recording be turned into an album.</p><p>“I had never thought about a commercial release. My whole idea was to keep a low profile about what I'd done,” Goldstein says.</p><p>Now that he’s gone public, however, Goldstein looks back on the recording — and its new place in jazz history — with pride.</p><p>“I have four grandchildren, ages 12 to 21, and I asked each of them separately, ‘Have you ever heard of Louis Armstrong?’ And all four of them said immediately, ‘Oh yes, of course,’” Goldstein says. “He supersedes jazz.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago extends street-sweeping to week before Christmas as leaves linger on city trees
entries.summary: <p>As leaves continue to fall across Chicago neighborhoods, residents have called on the city to keep its street sweepers out longer. </p><p>The city plans to continue its posted street-sweeping schedule through Dec. 17, nearly a month beyond its usual cutoff around Thanksgiving.</p><p>The extension will apply across all 50 wards, with crews prioritizing areas with heavier leaf coverage, said Cole Stallard, commissioner of the Chicago Department of Streets and Sanitation. The department has historically posted street-sweeping signs from April 1 until just before the week of Thanksgiving, when it pauses posted sweeping to avoid disrupting holiday visitors, he said.</p><p>In Rogers Park, Bill DeMarco, 65, told the Chicago Sun-Times that he recently saw leaves still clinging to many of the neighborhood's trees, with others scattered along streets and gutters. He estimated that roughly 70% of the trees he saw still featured leaves, many of them green or only beginning to change color.</p><p>DeMarco added that the frequency of street sweeping in his neighborhood has been difficult to predict.</p><p>“It seems to be sporadic, and there's no insight into how and when the streets are swept,” he said.</p><p>The department's traditional schedule was designed for a time when leaves fell earlier in the season, Stallard said. But this year, the signs of a changing fall were hard to miss. “You can just drive around the city and still see green leaves on trees,” he said.</p><p>DeMarco said he had not seen street sweepers on local streets since October. A permanent sign in his area still lists April 1 through Oct. 31 as the street-sweeping period, he said.</p><p>Those permanent signs will not be updated, the department said in a statement to the Sun-Times. Instead, the city will continue posting temporary orange signs ahead of scheduled neighborhood sweeps. </p><p>Stallard said crews will focus on areas with heavier leaf coverage, but the extension does not mean every street will be swept repeatedly through Dec. 17. The department follows predetermined routes, he said, and will not necessarily return to a neighborhood for a couple of weeks after it has already been swept.</p><p>The city will continue street sweeping when weather permits in the winter. The department typically deploys about 20 to 30 sweepers a day during winter, compared with about 50 during the regular season, Stallard said. Freezing ground temperatures and equipment maintenance can also limit winter operations.</p><p>On average, residents may see their streets swept about five times a year.</p><p>The department is also asking residents not to blow or rake leaves into the street. Instead, residents should bag leaves, place the bags near their garbage cans and call 311 to request collection.</p><p>The delayed leaf drop comes after an unusually warm fall and a summer marked by drought and flooding said Christy Rollinson, a senior scientist at The Morton Arboretum. Drought generally causes trees to shed their leaves earlier, while warmer fall temperatures can delay the process. The timing also varies by tree species and location, Rollinson said.</p><p>“There's an incredible amount of variation among different kinds of trees in different locations on whether they've dropped their leaves yet or not,” Rollinson said.</p><p>Peak leaf fall typically occurs during the first two weeks of November, she added. Although the variation among trees seems greater than usual this year, Rollinson cautioned that this fall is an outlier, partly influenced by an exceptionally strong El Niño. While fall seasons are generally expected to get warmer over time, she said future years will not necessarily look the same.</p>

entries.title: Bears predictions: Week 11 vs. Saints

Peanut Tillman had a 21-yard pick-six and a fumble recovery. <b>Season</b>: 4-5.</p><h3><b>Jason Lieser</b></h3><p><b>Bears, 30-13:</b> This is one of the worst defenses the Bears will face all season, and they'll make the most of it as they try to get back on track offensively. <b>Season:</b> 5-4.</p><h3><b>Scoop Jackson</b></h3><p><b>Bears, 24-10: </b>The lean-all-in on the run game returns. The set-up for the next seven-week set-up. <b>Season</b>: 5-4.</p><h3><b>Steve Greenberg</b></h3><p><b>Bears, 31-16:</b> The 3-6 Saints are as salty and tough as a sugary beignet fresh out of the oven. entries.title: An e-scooter law in Illinois takes effect Jan. 1. How it aims to make riding them safer
entries.summary: <p>This year, several people in Chicago have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/05/01/loved-ones-launch-fundraiser-for-venezuelan-teenager-killed-in-south-side-scooter-crash" target="_blank" >died</a> while riding e-scooters, including <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/04/alex-blacio-scooter-death-western" target="_blank" ><u>teenagers</u></a>. </p><p>This month alone, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/06/electric-scooter-driver-67-killed-in-collision-with-speeding-suv-in-north-park" target="_blank" ><u>two men</u></a>, ages 67 and 39, were killed in collisions with vehicles. Hundreds in Chicago have been <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/transportation/2026/06/05/scooter-teen-crash-death-lane-tech-high-school-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>injured</u></a> in e-scooter accidents in the past few years as ridership grows. A new Illinois law aims to make riding e-scooters and e-bikes safer.</p><h3><b>What’s the new Illinois e-scooter law that goes into effect Jan. 1?</b></h3><p>The law classifies any device capable of going faster than 28 mph as motor vehicles and subjects their operators to the state’s drunken driving laws, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/06/04/e-bike-moto-regulation-illinois-pritzker-giannoulias" target="_blank" ><u>Sun-Times reported</u></a>. Legislation passed in June and was signed by Gov. JB Pritzker in August. It seeks to address a rise in injuries among children using them.</p><p>Owners of those high-speed devices — which can include e-bikes, e-motos, e-scooters, electric unicycles, electric skateboards — will be required to have a driver’s license, carry insurance and register their vehicle with the state. They will not be allowed on bike paths and, in some cases, bike lanes.</p><p>The law creates consistent rules for the devices across the state, eliminating a growing and inconsistent patchwork of local ordinances.</p><h3><b>Are there age minimums for riders of e-scooters and e-bikes?</b></h3><p>Yes. The law strengthens existing age minimums for e-bike and e-scooter riders.</p><p>Class 1 and Class 2 e-bikes, which go up to 20 mph, must be operated by someone at least 15 years old, according to the law. Riders must be at least 16 years old for Class 3 e-bikes, which go up to 28 mph. E-scooter users must be at least 16 years old, and are capped at 15 mph.</p><p>Though Lime and Divvy require riders to be 18 or older — or at least 16 with parental consent — younger riders are still using them. An evaluation of the city’s 2020 e-scooter pilot program found that minors accounted for roughly 13% of reported injuries.</p><p>There are ways underage riders can get access to e-scooters, such as using an <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/cost-our-family-everything-parents-sound-alarm-after-teen-deaths-on-e-scooters/3942060/" target="_blank" ><u>adult’s account</u></a>.</p><h3><b>Are e-scooter accidents increasing?</b></h3><p>Yes. The Chicago Fire Department responded to nearly 200 e-scooter-related incidents in 2022. Within three years, that number had more than tripled, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/transportation/2026/06/05/scooter-teen-crash-death-lane-tech-high-school-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ reported</u></a>.</p><p>One national study found a 7.5-fold <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/graphics/2026/07/29/e-bike-injuries-child-kids-safety-health-transit/90956259007/" target="_blank" ><u>increase</u></a> in children on the vehicles seeking emergency care from 2023 to 2026.</p><p>But their popularity among teens — who are at times under the legal riding age — is growing as the city sees a rise in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/10/09/lime-divvy-chicago-e-scooter-riders-serious-injuries" target="_blank" >scooter-related crashes</a>, raising <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/05/04/chicago-launches-e-scooter-safety-campaign-in-wake-of-recent-scooter-deaths" target="_blank" >safety concerns</a> among doctors and city officials</p><h3><b>Has e-scooter ridership grown in Chicago?</b></h3><p>Yes. Chicago launched its first <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/6/11/18661876/electric-scooters-chicago-10-vendors-bird-bolt-gruv-jump-lime-lyft-sherpa-spin-veoride-wheels" target="_blank" >e-scooter pilot program</a> in 2019. By 2022, Lime and Divvy e-scooters became ubiquitous.</p><p>Lime, which is partially owned by Uber, has grown from operating 1,000 scooters in 2022 to 11,000 as of this past summer, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/transportation/2026/06/05/scooter-teen-crash-death-lane-tech-high-school-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ</u></a>. Divvy, operated by Lyft, has expanded its fleet to 2,800 e-scooters.</p><p>Combined, e-scooter ridership for these two companies totaled almost 7 million trips last year, according to the Chicago Department of Transportation.</p><p>More than 3.7 million trips were recorded on rental e-scooters between mid-2022 and late 2023, according to city data, compared with 1.3 million rides between 2019 and 2020, reported the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/10/09/lime-divvy-chicago-e-scooter-riders-serious-injuries" target="_blank" ><u>Sun-Times</u></a>.</p><h3><b>What is Chicago doing to make riding e-scooters safer?</b></h3><p>In May, the city of Chicago launched an e-scooter <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/05/04/chicago-launches-e-scooter-safety-campaign-in-wake-of-recent-scooter-deaths" target="_blank" ><u>safety campaign</u></a>. It included new rider safety messaging across the city and expanded scooter parking and bike infrastructure. The campaign also included stronger compliance requirements for operators and riders that will include stronger parking standards and expanded sidewalk-riding detection technology.</p>

entries.title: We are Chicago’s paper
entries.summary: <p>I still have the newspaper clipping dated July 19, 1995, from Chicago Sun-Times political cartoonist Jack Higgins. The single frame said: “CITY EMERGENCY HEALTH PLAN” inside a box of dotted lines which read “CUT HERE AND USE AS FAN.”</p><p>I lived through that summer’s fatal heat wave, when more than 700 people died. I was just a teenager, but I clipped that comic while reading the newspaper on the train and held onto it for 30 years. Many of the people who died were poor or older residents, and I was saddened thinking how my aging grandmother in her 80s might have fared had she lived here instead of two states away.</p><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Sun-Times was my newspaper back then. And today, as the Sun-Times’ editor-in-chief, I still call it my paper.</p><p>Thirty years since that fateful summer, the Sun-Times continues to offer the fiery critique, the provocative headlines, the accountability-driven investigations, the insider political coverage and the fly-on-the-wall sports coverage that captures the vibes of our city.</p><p>But some things do change. In 2018 we declared ourselves “The Hardest-Working Paper in America.” We’ll always be proud of our working-class roots. But we want to focus not just on our work but who we serve with that work. And we work for you, the people of Chicago. We always have, of course, but we want to clearly state where we’ve been and where we want to continue to go.</p><p>Today, you’ll see a new tagline on your paper: “Chicago’s paper.”</p><p>This is our commitment to Chicago and our belief that we will continue to serve as the primary news source for our region.</p><p>Four years ago, Chicago Public Media made a big bet acquiring the Chicago Sun-Times. The theory was that critical journalism would support our city. <a class="Link" href="https://www.rebuildlocalnews.org/local-news-shortage-leads-to-1-1-billion-in-extra-borrowing-costs-for-local-governments-and-taxpayers/" target="_blank" >Research</a> shows that when local papers close, voter participation and civic engagement decline, public spending increases due to waste, and there's more corruption and partisanship. We couldn't just let that happen. And our bet has paid off.</p><p>So we continue to build on what we do best: bringing you the trusted reporting and storytelling on sports, politics, investigations, community voices, arts and culture — but, perhaps most importantly, committing to the belief that a daily newspaper connects us together as a community.</p><p>Many of the things I’ve collected over the years have ended up in the trash — but not my old Jack Higgins cartoon. That remains intact, wedged between the glossy pages of a Jostens high school senior scrapbook. Though the clipping has outlasted many things, I’m glad our newspaper won’t be one of them.</p><p>Kimbriell Kelly<br>Editor-in-Chief<br>Chicago Sun-Times | WBEZ | vocalo.org | Chicago.com | Chicago Public Media</p>

And the future of the program remains uncertain.</p><p><b>What's ahead</b>: Galvanized by Democrats gaining the majority in Congress, Gov. At the same time, the Trump administration is reportedly proposing another change to SNAP that could further shrink eligibility.</p><p><b>Applications keep coming</b>: More Cook County residents entries.title: Man critically hurt in shooting, robbery along bike path on DuSable Lake Shore in Lake View
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for an assailant who robbed and shot a 35-year-old man in the head, critically wounding him late Wednesday along a Lake View bike path. </p><p>The man was found lying on the ground after police responded to a person shot about 10:40 p.m. in the 3300 block of North DuSable Lake Shore Drive, police said. </p><p>The man, shot in the head, was taken in critical condition to Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center, according to police. </p><p>Police say the victim's personal property was taken at the scene. </p><p>No arrests were made. </p><p>Area 3 detectives are investigating. </p>
entries.author: Christiana Freitag

entries.title: Woman fatally shot during homicide, man fatally shot in death investigation overnight in Rogers Park
entries.summary: <p>Police are investigating two fatal shootings in Rogers Park overnight. </p><p>Officers responding to a call of a person shot found a 24-year-old woman with a gunshot wound to the head about 11:15 p.m., police said. </p><p>She was dead at the scene and police are investigating her death as a homicide, according to police. </p><p>About two hours later and a half a mile away, a 25-year-old man was found dead with a gunshot wound in the stairwell of the Morse CTA Red Line station, at 1:05 a.m. at 1358 W. Morse Ave., according to police. </p><p>Police did not say the man's death was suspicious and detectives were considering it a death investigation. </p><p>It wasn't immediately clear if the two deaths were linked and their names have not been released by the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Area 3 detectives are probing both cases. </p>
entries.author: Christiana Freitag

Whether you are looking to advance at your barista job in Ravenswood, create more sophisticated window displays in the West Loop, or develop AI skills to take the next step in your career in South Shore, free training from Verizon can help you put artificial intelligence to work.

entries.title: Bulls' Matas Buzelis keeps having 'worst day' and that's a good thing
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK – Matas Buzelis sat in front of his locker last week, answering the same question the best he could.</p><p>Then again, how many different ways can a player try to explain why he’s not playing well?</p><p>The Bulls forward wasn’t, and the loss to San Antonio felt like rock bottom for Buzelis, earning him a second-half benching after he went scoreless in the third quarter with four turnovers.</p><p>“To be honest it’s on me,” Buzelis said then of the team’s struggles. “I have to be way better and I will be.”</p><p>A promise, a guarantee, or just a gut feeling.</p><p>It didn’t seem to matter much for Buzelis late Wednesday night. The Bulls were 2-1 on the three-city road trip after a laugher against the Brooklyn Nets and Buzelis had just put in an easy 25.</p><p>“Keep struggling,” Buzelis said.</p><p>That’s a saying going around the team courtesy of video coordinator Jeremiah Bonsu.</p><p>“I’m never the type to give up ever,” Buzelis explained. “I’ve come way too far, not going to give up. Actually, we have this saying from Jeremiah, it’s like, ‘Keep struggling, keep having the worst day. That’s how you build and get better.’</p><p>“My dedication to myself, how hard I work, I’m just going to go out there and trust my skills.”</p><p>But there is an elephant in the room that needs to be addressed, and that’s the fact that there is no longer a rookie in the room. Prized first-round pick Caleb Wilson went down with a broken right hand, and the bump up in numbers for Buzelis feels more than just coincidence.</p><p>In the first 10 games with Wilson, Buzelis averaged 13.5 points, 4.3 rebounds and 0.6 blocks per game, while shooting 31.4% from three-point range.</p><p>In the four games without Wilson, Buzelis has averaged 19.3 points, 5.8 rebounds and 1.3 blocks, while shooting 50% from three-point range. The Bulls went 3-1 in that time.</p><p>A reminder that before the hype of Wilson hit the city – hype that has been warranted – Buzelis, 22, put together a post-All-Star showcase last season in which he averaged 19 points, 6.9 rebounds and 1.6 blocks per game to close out the final 22 games.</p><p>“I think he’s just made the game easy, simpler, in terms of not playing into a crowd, finding guys, take open shots, attack the closeouts … you’re a great player,” coach Tiago Splitter said of Buzelis and his turnaround over the last week. “You’ve just got to be mindful of that, take good shots and don’t force it. We don’t need to force it. If you share the ball, move the ball from side to side everybody is going to eat and score.”</p><p>Buzelis was asked about putting up better numbers without Wilson out there but downplayed that as an explanation.</p><p>“Just playing man,” Buzelis said. “Nothing really (has changed). Just sharing the ball really well, credit to my teammates. We’re just playing basketball.</p><p>“I’m reading the game, playing, competing, and that’s about it. It was a whole new team so I was trying to figure out, ‘How can I attack all the closeouts?’ Because every team is different. But I’ve figured it out and I’m just going to keep it rolling.”</p><p>What was also a reminder in the wake of the Brooklyn win? Buzelis is a high-level competitor that, like Wilson has stated numerous times, is also chasing greatness.</p><p>“My mentality is always to go kill everyone,” Buzelis said. “That’s how I was trained. How my parents raised me was to go get it. We’re playing really well (lately), playing great basketball, and in the end that’s all that really matters.</p><p>“We’ve gotten into our rhythm. We know where other guys are, we know what we have to do, our role. It’s pretty simple. Basketball is a pretty simple game.”</p>

entries.title: Una mezquita de Berwyn recibe a la creciente comunidad musulmana latina del área
entries.summary: <p>Una iglesia que estuvo cerrada en Berwyn ahora es el hogar de una comunidad creciente de musulmanes latinos.</p><p>Durante años, los conversos latinos al islam en el área de Chicago lucharon por encontrar espacios religiosos y redes de apoyo que reflejaran tanto su fe como sus orígenes culturales.</p><p>Ese es el caso de Raúl González, que se crió pentecostal en Humboldt Park y se convirtió al islam hace 26 años.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b40000" name="module-b40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“El islam habla de la unidad de los creyentes, y por eso yo buscaba más hermanos, más gente como yo, latinos conversos al islam”, dijo.</p><p>Luego conoció a Christopher AbdulKareem Pavlicek, que sentía lo mismo, y empezaron a buscar un lugar donde los musulmanes que hablan español pudieran reunirse.</p><p>Lo encontraron en Berwyn, en esa iglesia cerrada.</p><p>“Así que necesitábamos juntarnos y, en realidad, establecer algo, dejar de ser huéspedes y empezar a ser anfitriones”, entries.title: Illinois officials fear a toxic lead-dust plume may spread from Army site explosion in Iowa
entries.summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker’s top <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment" >environmental</a> official is warning that a detonation of hazardous waste at a Department of Defense site in Iowa southwest of the Quad Cities could send lead dust into the air, creating a health threat to Illinois residents.</p><p>A public notice from the federal government Monday announced that there will be an unprecedented detonation of about 5 tons of hazardous materials at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, Friday between 11 a.m. and noon.</p><p>The notice describes the material designated to be exploded as “lead azide hazardous waste,” which is toxic. Lead azide is a chemical used in the production of bombs. The materials have to be destroyed because there's a chance they could explode if they are moved or even remain in storage, according to the Defense Department. </p><p>The explosion is expected to create a dust plume containing lead that may cross into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois" >Illinois</a>. Lead is toxic to humans and animals. It can be particularly harmful to children with developing brains and nervous systems. Health experts say there is no safe level of lead exposure.</p><p>“As we witnessed during this summer’s wildfire season, air pollution does not respect state lines and accordingly we strongly urge the Department of Defense to conduct comprehensive post-detonation environmental sampling,” James Jennings, director of the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency, said in a statement.</p><p>That testing, he added, should include “air, soil, and surface dust testing in potentially impacted areas of Illinois.”</p><p>Jennings asked Defense officials to share the test results with the public. The Illinois EPA will be monitoring air as well. It's unclear whether the lead dust could blow as far northeast as Chicago.</p><p>The notice from the Defense Department said it would be too dangerous to attempt to move the materials.</p><div drifting into Illinois after the U.S. Army announced a planned explosion in western Iowa.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>While the Army has destroyed weapons and materials in the past, it has never blown up such a large amount of this particular chemical, according to a spokesperson.</p><p>"We detonate all the time, but we have not detonated lead azide at this quantity," said Lori McFate, public affairs specialist with the Army Sustainment Command in Bettendorf, Iowa.</p><p>McFate said the explosion will take place after months of planning. The procedure has received a green light from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency regional office in Kansas City. That's a different jurisdiction than the regional EPA office in Chicago, which oversees environmental protection in Illinois. </p><p>The Army is advising nearby residents in Iowa that there will be a plume carrying elevated levels of lead. It recommends either evacuating or avoiding the area or remaining indoors with windows closed until Army officials give an all-clear notice.</p><p>“There is no safe level of lead in the body, and when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health" >health</a> risks,” Dr. Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, said in a statement. </p><p>“Illinois residents who may be affected by the detonation can stay safe by staying indoors and keeping windows closed for 24 to 48 hours. Washing your hands prior to eating and drinking, as well as washing outdoor surfaces with soap and water are ways to minimize exposure and limit the risk of tracking toxic residue into homes," he added.</p><p>For more information on the detonation, visit the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant's <a class="Link" href="https://www.army.mil/asc#org-iowa-army-ammunition-plant" target="_blank" >public notice site</a>.</p>

entries.title: NFL TV analyst rankings: Fox, CBS No. 2s are No. 1 quality
entries.summary: <p>Are you aware of the forthcoming football feast?</p><p>Next week, NFL games will appear on a TV near you on Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Sunday and Monday. That’s five out of six days with NFL action. That has to be a first in world history.</p><p>Those five days will feature seven stand-alone games on — try to follow me — Netflix, CBS, Fox, NBC, Prime Video and ESPN.</p><p>You might say that’s a lot of games. I say that’s a lot of broadcasters.</p><p>This season, analysts have been in the spotlight. It began with CBS dumping Tony Romo and promoting J.J. Watt. It continued with Troy Aikman feeling betrayed by Joe Buck — ESPN gave Buck a new contract, not Aikman — and the rapid rise of newcomers.</p><p>In that spirit, let’s do what this column does best — or at least does — rank things. The star of a football TV broadcast is supposed to be the analyst, like the great John Madden was. So let’s examine analysts. Here are our top 10, most of whom you’ll see next week.</p><h3>1. Greg Olsen, Fox</h3><p>Fox’s No. 2 analyst is No. 1 in my heart. If not for Tom Brady, Olsen still would be on the top crew with Kevin Burkhardt. Olsen is as enthusiastic and as knowledgeable as they come. He’s detail-oriented and is able to explain those intricacies succinctly. But don’t expect him to be with Fox much longer. With Aikman on the outs at ESPN and Watt on a first-team tryout at CBS, Olsen could be a No. 1 analyst again next season.</p><h3>2. Troy, Aikman, ESPN</h3><p>Speaking of Aikman, he has been the gold standard for years. A Hall of Fame quarterback and three-time Super Bowl champion, he has great insight and strong opinions. He isn’t afraid to call out anyone — even his partner. Though his 25-year run with Buck is nearing the end, they continue to put on a professional broadcast. If Aikman doesn’t join a team’s front office, he’ll be a No. 1 analyst elsewhere next season, perhaps competing with Olsen.</p><h3>3. Cris Collinsworth, NBC</h3><p>Collinsworth is a polarizing figure. Critics are nauseated by his adoration for particular players (cough, Patrick Mahomes, cough) and his tendency to spout what teams tell him when he should know better. But he has a keen eye, a sharp wit and opinions. Breaking down plays is great. Telling viewers what you think is even better.</p><h3>4. Tom Brady, Fox</h3><p>The GOAT quarterback is far from being the GOAT analyst — could anyone ever unseat Madden? — but he has the potential to be one of the best. He just needs to be more consistent. Brady has moments of sharp insight and others of useless interjections (“Ooohhh!”). Fox is paying him $375 million to use words. He’ll call Saints-Bears on Sunday.</p><h3>5. Drew Brees, Fox</h3><p>Brees has improved so much since he clammed up alongside Mike Tirico during a 2022 playoff game on NBC. He has given Fox great analyst depth after Brady and Olsen. Brees had a strong showing on the Vikings-Packers broadcast last week, particularly for explaining route combinations. He and Adam Amin have made a fine duo.</p><h3>6. Ross Tucker, CBS</h3><p>When Watt joined Jim Nantz on the top team, Tucker joined Ian Eagle on the second team. They had called “Thursday Night Football” together on Westwood One, and they picked up where they left off. Tucker, who also had been on CBS’ sixth crew, is excellent at breaking down blocking schemes as a rare former offensive lineman in the booth.</p><h3>7. J.J. Watt, CBS</h3><p>Watt blossomed last season as a rookie game analyst alongside Eagle. He hasn’t been quite as good this season as he tries to mesh with Nantz. That has led to the belief that Eagle brings out more in his partners than Nantz, particularly after Romo’s fall from grace. But Watt has his moments, such as Sunday when he caught Falcons right tackle Jawaan Taylor tipping plays.</p><h3>8. Kirk Herbstreit, Prime Video</h3><p>This was an odd hire from the start. It’s not that Herbstreit is bad at the job. It’s that he’s so embedded in ESPN’s coverage of college football, he can’t possibly be as attuned to the pro game as he needs to be. That comes through on the broadcast.</p><h3>9. Luke Kuechly, Netflix</h3><p>The former Panthers linebacker is the next rising star among NFL analysts. He’ll call the Packers-Rams game Wednesday with Noah Eagle. They called 49ers-Rams in Australia in Week 1, and Kuechly received positive reviews for astute, detailed analysis.</p><h3>10. Daryl Johnston, Fox</h3><p>Aikman gets a lot of plaudits for his longevity, but “Moose” has been in the booth just as long. He has been all over Fox’s depth chart, moving up to the No. 2 team when Buck and Aikman left the network. Johnston always has been solid. He doesn’t draw a lot of attention, which isn’t bad.</p><h3>REMOTE PATROL</h3><p><b>NBC 5 gets Bears on Netflix</b></p><p>On Christmas Day, Netflix will broadcast the Packers-Bears game, and fans who don’t subscribe to the streaming service will wonder where they can watch the game. The answer: NBC 5.</p><p>The NFL mandates that games carried by streamers or cable channels must air on over-the-air stations in the teams’ local markets. With NBC Sports handling the game production for Netflix, NBC 5 will carry the game in the Chicago market.</p><p>NBC 5 had the Bears’ game against the Buccaneers two weeks ago, and it has a chance for one more if the NFL flexes the Week 13 game against the Jaguars.</p><p><b>ESPN drops in-game ticker</b></p><p>When ESPN introduced the BottomLine in 1995, it was a revelation. But today, with everyone holding their phone while they watch games, is it necessary?</p><p>ESPN doesn’t think so. After initially removing the ticker from its college football broadcasts, the network has removed it from all live games across its networks. The BottomLine will appear during studio programming and to announce programming changes.</p><p>The network said removing the ticker provides a “cleaner presentation,” and that’s true, especially considering the size of its scorebugs. Smart move by the Worldwide Leader.</p>
