entries.title: Felony charges filed against motorist in May fatal hit-and-run in West Lawn
entries.summary: <p>A Clearing neighborhood man was due in court Thursday, facing felony charges for driving off after fatally hitting a man who was changing a tire in May on the Southwest Side. </p><p>Jan Rolon Valentin, 26, was arrested Wednesday after he was identified as the person who struck Enrique Nieto on May 12 in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/13/man-killed-in-west-lawn-hit-and-run" target="_blank" >6800 block of South Pulaski Road</a>, Chicago police said. </p><p>Nieto, 53, was changing a tire when he was struck by Valentin who was driving an orange Honda SUV and drove off, police said. </p><p>Nieto was taken to Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn where he was pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>Valentin, of the Clearing neighborhood, was charged with leaving the scene of an accident causing injury or death. </p><p>He was expected to appear in court Friday. </p>

entries.title: Review: The Neighbourhood plays up the past and future in United Center performance
entries.summary: <p>The glaringly bright and blinding white light emanating from the stage at United Center Wednesday night could only mean one of two things: We'd either all crossed over or, maybe more realistically, we were witnessing an alien takeover.</p><p>At least that’s what The Neighbourhood wanted everyone to believe as singer Jesse Rutherford descended from “outer space,” decked in a skin-tight aluminum space suit and silver body paint. His mission: to deliver transmissions from the band’s Ziggy Stardust-esque concept album “Chip Chrome & the Mono-Tones.”</p><p>The alt rock band committed to the bit for the first six numbers, starting with sad song “Pretty Boy” through the maniacal funk of “Devil’s Advocate.” </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7691341/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F06%2F60618c894ac3b4114c9e0553a432%2Ftheneighbourhood-261119-17.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bcea18c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F06%2F60618c894ac3b4114c9e0553a432%2Ftheneighbourhood-261119-17.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7691341/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffb%2F06%2F60618c894ac3b4114c9e0553a432%2Ftheneighbourhood-261119-17.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Singer Jesse Rutherford descends from “outer space,” decked in a skin-tight aluminum space suit and silver body paint, Wednesday during The Neighbourhood’s show at United Center. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The two parties were separated by a white picket fence that was part of the suburban sprawl on stage, also including the band’s familiar upside-down house motif. But Rutherford is no Bowie, and as the front man awkwardly distanced himself from the incredibly skilled ensemble (guitarists Jeremy Fredman and Zach Abels, bassist Mikey Margott, drummer Brandon Fried and a few touring members), it only amplified the fact that the singer was on his own weird island.</p><p>Resuscitating Chip Chrome was an odd choice to lead off the band’s largely sold-out World Tour. The 2020 album is light-years-old at this point, and its themes of struggling with identity and social media obsession were moot with the entire arena recording and posting the show from their cellphones. Adding to the oddball eccentricity, The Neighbourhood used the short set to open the band's own set — even though Nessa Barrett and Noise Dept. (the project of Neighbourhood touring member Raj Jain) already did a fine job at that.</p><p>After 30 minutes, the house lights and house music came back on as crews did a sweep of the stage, preparing for the real (and much better) show to begin. When the band returned, the dividers were gone and Rutherford had scrubbed away the tin man from his skin as the group launched into The Neighbourhood’s moody greatest hits. Among them, “Afraid,” “Reflections,” “Daddy Issues” and the queen bee, “Sweater Weather,” appropriately at the time of year when everyone starts putting the song on repeat. (There’s a new seasonal track, the holiday tune “Why’d You Have to Leave,” though the band did not play it.) </p><p>All the traction behind “Sweater Weather” has allowed The Neighbourhood’s signature track to make history this year. In August, it entered the billions club on YouTube and, this month, it made Spotify history as the third song ever to surpass 5 billion streams. Not too shabby for a 14-year-old number that’s nearly as old as the band itself, which was founded in 2011 in Newbury Park, California (don’t let the British spellings used on nearly everything confuse you about the band’s origin).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-000000" name="image-000000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/751f19d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6e%2Fef%2Fb480bb8147c6878ef5f4d9004e9c%2Ftheneighbourhood-261119-32.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b08b664/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6e%2Fef%2Fb480bb8147c6878ef5f4d9004e9c%2Ftheneighbourhood-261119-32.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/26be99d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6e%2Fef%2Fb480bb8147c6878ef5f4d9004e9c%2Ftheneighbourhood-261119-32.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The Neighborhood front man Jesse Rutherford performs Wednesday at United Center. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/26be99d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6e%2Fef%2Fb480bb8147c6878ef5f4d9004e9c%2Ftheneighbourhood-261119-32.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6cbc1f5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6e%2Fef%2Fb480bb8147c6878ef5f4d9004e9c%2Ftheneighbourhood-261119-32.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/26be99d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6e%2Fef%2Fb480bb8147c6878ef5f4d9004e9c%2Ftheneighbourhood-261119-32.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Neighborhood front man Jesse Rutherford performs Wednesday at United Center. The first six songs of the band’s set was a nod to its Ziggy Stardust-esque concept album “Chip Chrome & the Mono-Tones.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Neighbourhood has seen a resurgence in recent years, driven by a TikTok algorithm jackpot that has introduced the band to a new generation who have used “Sweater Weather” and the other late-bloomer viral track “Daddy Issues” as jumping-off points to dive into the full catalog. Kids who weren’t even born when the group debuted were a big part of the mix at the UC, turning every song into a sing-along and screaming every time their favorite track was played or when Rutherford took off his leather jacket, bearing an armor of tattoos. There was a similar effect at Lollapalooza over the summer when the band drew swarms to the T-Mobile stage, even as they were forced to play a stripped-down set due to instruments and gear that were delayed in-flight.</p><p>That wasn’t the case at United Center Wednesday as the band came fully prepared with its musical army that went to battle delivering a luscious, textured palette of alt rock, R&B, hip-hop and synth pop that have become The Neighbourhood’s standard. From slower ballads like “Lovebomb” to the cinematic beauty of “Baby Came Home 2,” it was a hypnotic spiral of sounds that flowed so well, it made you forget the band was introducing newer music, too.</p><p>Last November, The Neighbourhood released “Ultrasound,” its first album after a multi-year hiatus that began in 2022 when Brandon Fried was initially fired over sexual assault allegations, as the group cited a "zero tolerance policy" and debated its future. After public apologies and a stint in rehab, Fried was controversially reinstated and appeared on stage Wednesday. The band barely talked to the crowd Wednesday night, but Rutherford briefly addressed the break. “Thanks for sticking with us all this time and all these years,” he said, “we won’t take so long next time.”</p><p>As The Neighbourhood navigates this latest phase, the question will be if it can keep the momentum going and meet the demand of an arena-level act. The band returns to the United Center May 8 for World Tour II, which is a good sign. But maybe next time they should leave the spaceship at home and blind audiences with their natural light instead.</p><p></p><h3>Set list for The Neighbourhood at United Center Nov. 18, 2026</h3><h3></h3><p>Pretty Boy<br>Lost in Translation<br>Stargazing<br>Fallen Star<br>Cherry Flavoured<br>Devil's Advocate</p><p><i>-Set Break-</i></p><p>Start<br>Afraid<br>You Get Me So High<br>Reflections<br>R.I.P. 2 My Youth<br>Zombie<br>Cry Baby<br>Void<br>Lovebomb<br>Holy Ghost<br>A Little Death<br>Daddy Issues<br>Baby Came Home 2<br>The Beach<br>Hula Girl<br>Private<br>Sweater Weather<br>Softcore</p>

entries.title: Bears practice report: DT Jeffery Simmons returns, expected to play vs. Saints
entries.summary: <p>What happened Thursday at Halas Hall:</p><p><b>Simmons rolling</b><br><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons was back at practice after missing Tuesday with what the team labeled a knee injury. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said he did not “anticipate any issues” regarding his availability to play Sunday against the Saints.</p><p><b>Gordon still out </b><br>It’s much less promising for nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon, who missed his third consecutive practice with a shoulder injury. Gordon got hurt Nov. 8 against the Buccaneers and played through it, but is in doubt for Sunday. He has missed 19 games over the last two seasons.</p><p><b>Top seller</b><br>Bears quarterback Caleb Williams’ No. 18 jersey <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/19/bears-qb-caleb-williams-has-top-selling-jersey-on-fanatics-for-first-month-of-nfl-season" >was the leading seller on Fanatics</a> for the first half of the season. entries.title: Cook County Jail wrongful death lawsuit settles for record $7.25 million
entries.summary: <p><i>This story was produced by </i><a class="Link" href="http://injusticewatch.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Injustice Watch</i></a><i>, a nonprofit newsroom in Chicago that investigates issues of equity and justice in the Cook County court system. </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/subscribe/" target="_blank" ><i>Sign up here to get their weekly newsletter</i></a><i>.</i></p><p>The family of a man with mental illness who died at the Cook County Jail after being beaten by correctional officers has agreed to dismiss a wrongful death lawsuit against the county in exchange for $7.25 million.</p><p>The Cook County Board of Commissioners approved the deal Thursday, making it the county’s largest single payout for a jail-related lawsuit since at least 2007, according to an Injustice Watch analysis of settlement data.</p><p>The lawsuit revolves around <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/06/28/cook-county-jail-detainee-death-cory-ulmer-beating-handcuffed-sheriff-tom-dart" >the death of 41-year-old Cory Ulmer</a> in June 2024. Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart’s office, which runs the jail, told Ulmer’s family only that he died following a medical emergency, but <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/jail-deaths/2024/cook-county-jail-cory-ulmer-death/" target="_blank" >an internal report</a> leaked to Injustice Watch just days after his demise showed officers repeatedly struck him in the jail’s emergency room after Ulmer became “combative.”</p><p>Records obtained since then show the sheriff’s internal investigators found several officers committed misconduct against Ulmer, with two officers now facing termination. One of those officers had been recommended for firing a decade ago but was allowed to remain on the job, records show.</p><p>Officers began striking Ulmer after he tried running out of a small, bedless holding cell in the jail’s basement known as a “bullpen,” where he had been kept for at least 24 hours awaiting transfer to a psychiatric unit, records show. Officers then dragged Ulmer into the emergency room and witnesses told investigators the officers proceeded to kick, punch, and knee him as he lay facedown, shackled and facing away from security cameras, records show. Ulmer was then injected with sedatives and became unresponsive and was declared dead upon arrival soon after at Mount Sinai Hospital, records show. The Cook County medical examiner ruled his death a homicide.</p><p>Ulmer was taken to jail just a day before he died for violating his court-ordered curfew following 2023 assault and armed robbery charges. The arresting officers with the sheriff’s electronic monitoring unit noted Ulmer was unwell; he was walking on the road shirtless after midnight, and one of the officers speculated Ulmer was “off his meds,” records show. The officers considered taking Ulmer home or to a hospital but took him to the jail instead, records show.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> he died in June 2024. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>llinois State Police</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ulmer’s stepfather, Robert Robinson, <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/jail-deaths/2025/family-sues-cook-county-sheriff-tom-dart-over-brutal-jail-death/" target="_blank" >sued the county</a> in federal court last year, alleging the officers used excessive force against Ulmer in violation of his constitutional rights and that the jail’s medical staff failed to provide him with adequate care or antipsychotic medications, “despite obvious signs that his mental state was deteriorating.” In court filings, the county denied those allegations.</p><p>Ulmer died less than two weeks after Injustice Watch published <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/jail-deaths/2024/cook-county-jail-deaths-2023/" target="_blank" >“Dying on Dart’s Watch,”</a> which revealed inadequate medical care and supervision underlying at least half of the 18 deaths at the jail in 2023. That was the most deaths there in any year since 2013, when the jail’s average daily population was twice as high.</p><p>Since Ulmer’s death, at least another 28 detainees have died at the jail, records show.</p><p>In a statement, Robinson’s attorney, Jesse Guth, said there was “no excuse for the brutality that Cory suffered” and called on lawmakers to open the jail to independent monitoring, to review conditions at the facility for detainees.</p><p>“History will continue to repeat itself until changes are implemented,” Guth said.</p><p>Dart handily won another four-year term in this month’s general election. Citing pending litigation, he declined to be interviewed, as did Dr. Priscilla Ware, medical director of the jail’s healthcare provider, Cermak Health Services. Ware was not a defendant in the lawsuit.</p><h3>Firings, suspensions held up in arbitration</h3><p>The sheriff’s Office of Professional Review closed its internal investigation into Ulmer’s death in December 2025, a year and a half after he died, records show. Investigators probed the actions of 18 correctional officers and said two should be fired and six should be suspended.</p><p>Of the 11 medical staffers named in the lawsuit, one has since left the jail, records show. The others — including doctors, nurses and mental health specialists — continued to work there as of late October. In response to emailed questions, a spokesperson for Cermak Health Services, a division of Cook County Health, did not say whether any of the medical staff had been disciplined.</p><p>Investigators recommended that Sgt. Enrique Reyes and correctional officer Jason Jackson be terminated from their jobs at the jail, records show. Injustice Watch could not reach Reyes and Jackson directly. Their attorneys did not respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Both used unnecessary force against Ulmer, investigators found; a medical staff member who witnessed the beating told investigators that Jackson hit Ulmer the most, and even kicked him in the head multiple times. Investigators also found that Reyes told medical staff to “leave the area” and turned off his body-worn camera during the incident. Reyes told investigators he turned his camera off because Ulmer was about to receive medical attention, but investigators found that to be untrue, records show.</p><p>Jackson’s fate now lies with the sheriff’s Merit Board, a seven-member body appointed by Dart and approved by a majority of county commissioners with final say over firings of correctional officers. Reyes’ firing is before an arbitrator, as is required by the correctional sergeant’s union contract, according to Dart’s spokesperson. In the meantime, both have been stripped of their police powers and were assigned to work at a warehouse, the spokesperson said.</p><p>Reyes and Jackson had each been investigated for misconduct several times prior to Ulmer’s death, according to data provided by Dart’s office through a public records request.</p><p>Investigators recommended that Jackson be fired a year after he was hired in 2016 for allowing detainees to enter a visiting area without permission, and failing to stop those detainees from masturbating in view of visitors. However, his case was instead handled by an arbitrator, who ruled that Dart’s office should reinstate Jackson six months later, according to the sheriff’s spokesperson.</p><p>“Given the fact that Jackson was suspended without pay for approximately 140 workdays … the Sheriff’s Office considered his unpaid suspension to be appropriate disciplinary action and did not initiate further proceedings,” the spokesperson said in a statement.</p><p>The sheriff’s internal investigators would go on to sustain misconduct allegations against Jackson in four more disciplinary cases for several policy violations such as using unnecessary force and threatening another person with bodily harm, records show.</p><p>Reyes was investigated on allegations he used excessive force in 2012, 2013, 2014, and 2021, and for allegedly failing to follow policy in 2023. Investigators either exonerated him, closed the investigation without a disposition, or did not sustain the allegations, data show.</p><p>The other six officers with sustained misconduct allegations in Ulmer’s investigation face suspensions ranging from 45 to 120 days for using unnecessary force and being untruthful to investigators, among other policy violations, records show. So far, only one officer has served a suspension, and an arbitrator reduced it from 45 days to five; the rest are still in arbitration, Dart’s spokesperson said. According to investigators, three of those officers failed to report a separate use of force against Ulmer on the morning of the day he died. That incident resulted in Ulmer falling and hitting the back of his head; it was discovered only after the jail’s surveillance team reviewed all of Ulmer’s movements from that day, records show.</p><p>Representatives for the correctional officers’ union, Teamsters Local 700, did not respond to requests for comment. A spokesperson for the correctional sergeants’ union, AFSCME Council 31 Local 3692, said the union does not answer questions about pending grievances.</p><p>Dart’s internal investigators did not look into why jail officials failed to notify the Cook County medical examiner when Ulmer died, records show.</p><p>Under county code, law enforcement officers should “immediately” notify the medical examiner upon a death in custody. The medical examiner then dispatches investigators to the scene to take photos, conduct interviews, and produce a report. The medical examiner was instead notified by a Mount Sinai nurse nearly six hours after Ulmer was pronounced dead, records show. By then, the jail’s emergency room, where officers beat him, had been cleaned.</p><p>In an email, Dart’s spokesperson did not deny jail officials failed to notify the medical examiner but said the sheriff’s office “worked to support every independent investigation conducted by outside agencies in this case.”</p><p>Jail officials enacted a dozen policy changes and directives following Ulmer’s death, including installing cameras to eliminate blind spots in the jail’s hospital, and instructing staff to provide water to detainees in the bullpen, records show.</p><h3></h3><h3>Growing calls for independent oversight</h3><p>The vote to settle the Ulmer lawsuit comes alongside calls for more oversight of the jail and the sheriff’s office.</p><p>Currently, only the Illinois Department of Corrections provides external monitoring of the jail through its jail and detention standards unit, which conducts annual inspections of the facility and issues yearly reports. But advocates and their allies on the Cook County Board of Commissioners say more oversight of the jail is needed to protect people incarcerated there.</p><p>Matthew McLoughlin, a campaign coordinator with the Illinois Network for Pretrial Justice, a coalition working to reduce the number of people incarcerated in jails across the state, said commissioners need more than the once-a-year reports to better understand the conditions in the Cook County Jail. An independent oversight body “would allow for that kind of regular communication,” he told Injustice Watch in an interview.</p><p>In 2025, state inspectors found the jail “violated standards for supervision, security, admissions procedures, reporting, sanitation and more,” the Illinois Answers Project <a class="Link" href="https://illinoisanswers.org/2026/09/15/unsanitary-unsupervised-understaffed-most-illinois-jails-arent-meeting-minimum-state-standards/" target="_blank" >reported</a> in September. Inspectors have cited the jail for violations in six of the past nine years, including every year since 2022, the nonprofit newsroom reported.</p><p>“Obviously, four years in a row of failed inspections, the accountability is not there,” McLoughlin said.</p><p>In an email, Dart’s spokesperson pushed back against the characterization of the sheriff’s office as having “failed” inspections, stressing that inspectors had found the jail to be in compliance with the vast majority of state standards each year.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ca55f45/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F48%2F88%2F1551a8f30d9d0015803a29e019c7%2Fmerlin-90700825.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/996645b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F48%2F88%2F1551a8f30d9d0015803a29e019c7%2Fmerlin-90700825.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ca55f45/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5472x3071+0+288/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F48%2F88%2F1551a8f30d9d0015803a29e019c7%2Fmerlin-90700825.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart speaks at a news conference in March 2020 about plans for the Cook County Jail during the COVID-19 pandemic. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Brian Rich/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The jail was previously subject to independent monitoring as part of a series of federal consent decrees, but those ended in 2017. Meanwhile, jails in cities including New York, Los Angeles, Denver, and Philadelphia are currently under some form of oversight aside from regulatory inspections, research shows.</p><p>In September, Cook County Commissioner Tara Stamps and four co-sponsors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/09/21/cook-county-jail-deaths-commissioners-board" >introduced a resolution</a> calling for an “independent review” of the jail, “focusing on the health, safety and wellness of the detainees and conditions of confinement.” The resolution came nearly two years after <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/jail-deaths/2024/sheriff-tom-dart-county-board-hearing-on-jail-deaths/" target="_blank" >the board held a hearing</a> on jail deaths following Injustice Watch’s reporting. But <a class="Link" href="https://illinoisanswers.org/2026/09/22/cook-county-board-defers-resolution-calling-for-independent-review-of-states-largest-jail/" target="_blank" >Stamps pulled the resolution</a> from a vote in the board’s Health and Hospitals Committee because her colleagues said it could prove to be a legal liability, the Illinois Answers Project reported.</p><p>Injustice Watch obtained an analysis of the resolution done by Cathy McNeil Stein, civil actions bureau chief for the Cook County state’s attorney’s office, and sent to county commissioners a day before they were set to vote. Stein said Stamps’ resolution would be “harmful” to the county’s legal position in pending and future litigation, and would increase its “financial jeopardy.”</p><p>Even if the resolution passed, Stein wrote, the board could not unilaterally order Dart to open the jail to an independent monitor, as state law says Illinois sheriffs have “final policymaking authority over jails in their counties,” citing state law and a circuit court ruling out of DuPage County.</p><p>Stamps told the Illinois Answers Project that she would “retool” and reintroduce the resolution this month, but she had not done so as of publication of this article.</p><p>In an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/11/11/cook-county-jail-independent-review-jamar-boyd-tariq-el-amin-rachel-mikva" target="_blank" >op-ed</a> for the Chicago Sun-Times published last week, a group of interfaith clergy called on commissioners to advance Stamps’ resolution. “The public deserves a clear explanation of how delaying an independent review serves the interests of those in custody and the broader community,” they wrote.</p><p>Stamps did not respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Meanwhile, Dart’s office has also recently come under scrutiny by Tirrell J. Paxton, the county’s independent inspector general.</p><p>In September, records show, Paxton issued six recommendations to the sheriff’s office after a review of more than 100 complaints forwarded to the sheriff’s Office of Professional Review by Paxton and his predecessors found that although the office “generally takes appropriate action,” there were “recurring deficiencies in investigative consistency, documentation, and case management.”</p><p>Dart’s general counsel, Nicholas Scouffas, fired back at Paxton, saying Paxton “did not possess the requisite information, data, understanding, wherewithal, and authority” to make the recommendations, and that the sheriff’s office rejected all of them.</p><p>The county board is now weighing whether to hold a hearing on Paxton’s potential oversight; it has also asked the state’s attorney’s office to provide a legal opinion of the matter.</p><p>Jennifer Vollen-Katz, executive director of prison watchdog group John Howard Association of Illinois, which monitored the jail from 1988 to 2011, told Injustice Watch that more oversight of the jail would ultimately reduce the county’s exposure to lawsuits and “can identify the policies and practices that are leading to these kinds of horrific outcomes that are costing people their lives and costing the taxpayers millions of dollars.”</p><p>“Sometimes just knowing you’re being watched prevents people from behaving badly,” Vollen-Katz said.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-390000" entries.title: CATCH-22: Bears won't curb celebrations after Aidan Hutchinson's 'freak' injury
entries.summary: <p>Analyzing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> with the help of 22 names, starting with …</p><p></p><p><b>Jahdae Walker (1)</b>, the wide receiver who, despite having three career touchdowns, is the Bears’ player most synonymous with celebrations. Since he was a sophomore in college, Walker was done the “Jubi Slide,” a dance in which skips he skips quickly to his left, giving the illusion he’s gliding along the field after a score. In his free time, he plans team-wide touchdown celebrations.</p><p></p><p>I asked Walker this week whether the injury to Lions defensive end <b>Aidan Hutichinson (2), </b>who<b> </b>tore his ACL Sunday while celebrating a sack, made him reconsider such elaborate displays.</p><p></p><p>“I’ve practiced them countless times — my celebrations are less likely to get me hurt,” Walker said.</p><p></p><p>He called Hutchinson’s injury a “freak accident,” and his teammates agreed. The Bears took no joy in a rival getting hurt, particularly in the way he did.</p><h3>The celebration was reminiscent of …</h3><p></p><p>“It’s all part of the play,” receiver <b>Rome Odunze</b> <b>(3)</b> said. “He’s gotta get up and get his teammates going. That’s his celebration. That’s his signature … That’s freaky.”</p><p></p><p>Lions coach <b>Dan Campbell (4)</b> said this week that he wouldn’t tell his team to tamp down their celebrations — "We're not talking to 8-year-olds here,” he said — but some around the league have taken heed. Giants running back <b>Cam Skattebo (5)</b>, notorious for his reckless running, said he was retiring his signature backflip touchdown celebration after watching Hutchinson get hurt.</p><p></p><p>Bears defensive end <b>Daniel Hardy (6)</b> waves his arms and hips in rhythm like wrestler <b>Jeff Hardy (7) </b>. He won’t change the way he celebrates. Football players don't tend to be cowed when others get injured — if they did, no one would make it to the end of the season.</p><h3>Still incredulous Thursday was …</h3><p></p><p>“Seeing someone get hurt in football, are you going to play less aggressive?” he said. “Probably not.”</p><p></p><h3>The celebration was reminiscent of …</h3><p></p><p>Former Bears defensive end <b>Lamarr Houston (8)</b>, who did a similar sack celebration in which he jumped in the air, landed and thrust his arms and hips forward. The Bears were trailing the Patriots by 25 in the fourth quarter in 2014 when Houston sacked backup quarterback <b>Jimmy Garoppolo (9) </b>and tore his knee with his sack dance.</p><p></p><p>“I probably shouldn’t have celebrated like that,” he said after the game.</p><h3>Bombing atomically on Thursday will be …</h3><p></p><h3></h3><p></p><p>Amazingly, Lions linebacker <b>Stephen Tulloch (10)</b> tore his knee just weeks prior to Houston doing the exact same celebration. Tulloch told the Detroit Free Press afterward that he didn’t regret the sack dance.</p><p></p><p>“I’d do it again, brother,” he said.</p><p></p><p>Twelve years later, Garoppolo has been floated as a potential replacement for <b>Drake Maye (11)</b>, who broke his ankle on the sack that Hutchinson celebrated, when the Patriots return from their bye.</p><p></p><h3>Still incredulous Thursday was …</h3><h3>Sharing the same birthday are …</h3><p></p><p>Bears receivers coach <b>Antwaan Randle El (12)</b>, when asked about Odunze’s two high-profile drops this year — against the Eagles and Bucs.</p><p></p><p>“It’s crazy that he’s had them,” he said. “Can’t explain it.”</p><p></p><p>When his players drop passes, Randle El tries to reset them on the sideline using a trick taught him by former NFL receivers coach <b>Jim Hostler (13)</b>.</p><p></p><p>“I have a guy do something normal,” he said.</p><p></p><p>Players drink out of squeeze bottles in games but out of cups outside of football. So he’ll have players who dropped a pass sip water out of a cup on the sideline to see if that changes their mindset — or their mojo.</p><p></p><p>“I started doing that in Detroit,” Randle El said. “I liked it; it worked.”</p><p></p><h3>Bombing atomically on Thursday will be …</h3><h3>null</h3><p>The Wu-Tang Clan. The nine-man rap powerhouse, which was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in Los Angeles last weekend, will perform the halftime show for the Bears-Lions game on Thanksgiving Day.</p><p></p><p>The group was chosen by Detroit’s own <b>Eminem</b> <b>(14)</b>, who helps produce the Lions’ Thanksgiving halftime shows and will be in attendance.</p><p></p><p>“I might steal a couple minutes and walk out and listen to them,” cornerback <b>Tyrique Stevenson (15)</b> said with a smile.</p><p></p><p>Hearing this, safety <b>Cam Lewis</b> <b>(16)</b> told Stevenson he knew nothing about the Staten Island, N.Y.-born rappers, whose album “Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers)” debuted in 1993. He asked what year Stevenson was born. The answer: 2000.</p><p></p><p>“I still grew up with their cassette tape,” Stevenson said.</p><p></p><p>The NFL’s halftime slate next week is top-notch, with U2 playing the Packers-Rams game on Wednesday night, <b>Miranda Lambert (17)</b> performing during the Cowboys-Eagles game on Thursday afternoon and Goo-Goo Dolls — with Buffalo-born singer <b>John Rzeznik (18) — </b>playing during the Chiefs-Bills game on Thursday night.</p><p></p><p>Eminem joined rock star <b>Jack White (19)</b> on stage last year for the Lions’ halftime show.</p><p></p><h3>Sharing the same birthday are …</h3><p></p><p>Two of the Bears’ best players: quarterback <b>Caleb Williams (20)</b> and guard <b>Joe Thuney (21). </b>On Wednesday, the Bears’ day off, Williams turned 25 and Thuney 34. Offensive line coach <b>Dan Roushar (22) </b>said with a smile Thuney showed up to work grumpy Thursday.</p><p></p><p>“We said there’s a big difference between 33 and 34,” he joked.</p>

entries.title: NITA releases unified safety reporting app for CTA, Metra and Pace
entries.summary: <p>Riders of CTA, Metra and Pace can now report crimes and concerns through a centralized smartphone app.</p><p>The Northern Illinois Transit Authority released the app, called NITA Ride Safe, on Thursday.</p><p>The app allows users to report safety incidents or concerns without calling a hotline or drawing attention to themselves. Users can send reports by text and photos. They have the option to remain anonymous.</p><p>The idea behind the app is to allow riders to discreetly report incidents that are not life-threatening, according to NITA. Those incidents can include harassment, threatening or disruptive behavior, like smoking, a suspicious or unattended item, drug use, vandalism or a person in crisis.</p><p>NITA still wants riders to call 911 for more serious incidents, like if someone is hurt or in immediate danger, a weapon is being used or a fire is spreading.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Screenshots of the new NITA Safe Ride app</p></figcaption></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The app is an updated version of Metra's COPS app, which has allowed its riders to report safety concerns since 2019. Reports sent through NITA Ride Safe will be answered by Metra staff who had been handling the COPS app, officials said in a previous NITA board meeting. Those employees will determine if a response requires police, CTA's new <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/08/12/cta-crisis-intervention-safe-ride-specialist-pilot" target="_blank" >Safe Ride Specialists</a>, other first responders or a customer service agent. Officials said the employees would be able to handle the expected increase in reports.</p><p>Riders without the app can report safety incidents by texting 312-313-9015.</p><p>NITA released the app days before the agency was required by law to have one. The app is one of several public safety requirements baked into the NITA Act, which requires the agency centralize coordination around public safety.</p><p>NITA is in the process of hiring a chief transit safety officer to lead a new Office of Transit Safety and Experience.</p><p>By next month, a NITA law enforcement task force, led by the Cook County Sheriff's Office, must share a report on whether to recommend the agency create its own police department. The NITA board must vote by next June on that recommendation.</p><p>Chicago-area transit officials have prioritized public safety over the last year, following a series of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/11/19/terrorism-charges-filed-after-woman-lit-on-fire-on-blue-line-in-loop" target="_blank" >high profile attacks</a>, historically high <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/02/chicago-cta-transit-crime-assault-battery-leerhsen" target="_blank" >reports of batteries</a> on the CTA, a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/12/19/president-trump-chicago-cta-crime-security-funding-cut-mayor-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" >funding threat</a> from the U.S. Department of Transportation, and riders reporting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/03/19/rta-nita-board-security-survey-cta-metra-pace" target="_blank" >safety as their top priority</a> for NITA.</p><p>In late 2025, the CTA began <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/12/18/cpd-officers-cta-surge-plan-security-crime" target="_blank" >increasing</a> the number of Chicago police officers and private security guards on transit. Last spring, sheriff's deputies were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/03/10/chicago-transit-authority-cta-crime-security-plan-fta" target="_blank" >deployed</a> on CTA trains and buses. Since then, CTA officials have reported a steady <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/07/08/cta-transit-crime-security-surge" target="_blank" >decline</a> of reported crimes.</p>

entries.title: 20 questions and answers on the upcoming Illinois high school basketball season
entries.summary: <p>Twenty questions and answers on the upcoming high school basketball season.</p><p><b>1. Who is the best player in the Chicago area?</b></p><p>Bolingbrook guard Brady Pettigrew emerged as a top 10 player in the country's junior class over the summer. He has his pick of schools with 36 scholarship offers and could realistically head to college after this season.</p><p><b>2. Which players are on the preseason All-State Team?</b></p><p>Pettigrew, Neuqua Valley junior Cole Kelly and senior Illinois recruit Mason Martin, Benet’s 6-8 senior Ed Stasys and Peoria Richwoods junior guard Amarion Smith-Holley.</p><p><b>3. Which teams are the favorites to win Class 4A</b></p><p>Neuqua Valley, Benet, Bolingbrook and Evanston open the season as the favorites. But those first three teams will all likely be in the same sectional.</p><p><b>4. Which teams could make a Cinderella run in Class 4A?</b></p><p>None of the four favorites are heavy favorites, and the field of contenders is large. St. Laurence and St. Ignatius are just a tick below that group, and it is not hard to imagine Lockport or Glenbrook North advancing to the state semifinals.</p><p><b>5. Who are the favorites in Class 3A?</b></p><p>East St. Louis, Peoria Richwoods, Centralia, Leo and Metamora make up the top tier of contenders.</p><p><b>6. What about Class 2A and 1A?</b></p><p>Peoria Manual is the 2A favorite, but Crane, Phillips and Farragut are legitimate contenders. Marshall, the defending Class 1A champs, returns nearly its entire team and is a major favorite to repeat.</p><p><b>7. Which players are worth traveling to see?</b></p><p>Pettigrew and Kelly are the only proven superstars in the state right now. Oswego junior Ethan Vahl has a crowd-pleasing style of play.</p><p><b>8. Which player has improved the most since last season?</b></p><p>No new star blossomed out of nowhere over the summer, but Stasys and St. Laurence senior Markese Peoples both took their games to a higher level.</p><p><b>9. Which freshman is a budding superstar?</b></p><p>There may not be a breakout superstar, but the class of 2030 appears strong, with several players expected to contribute to varsity teams this season. Bloom’s Larry Ellis, Bolingbrook’s Layton Jones, Kenwood’s Elijah McKinnie, Robert Smith Jr. and DJ Moore of Marist, Rantoul’s 6-10 Isaiah Stewart and Bloomington’s Brysen Morris are expected to make significant impacts.</p><p><b>10. Who is the most important transfer?</b></p><p>Senior guard Michael Woods' arrival vaulted Perspectives-Leadership into the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-basketball-rankings/2026/11/17/michael-obriens-preseason-super-25-illinois-high-school-basketball-rankings" >preseason Super 25</a>. JJ Duffin joining Peoria Richwoods and Nate Woods transferring to Bolingbrook elevated those teams' status.</p><p><b>11. Who are the most under-appreciated players in the area?</b></p><p>Hayden Schroeder, a 6-7 senior at Wheaton Academy, hasn’t received much attention but recently signed with Penn and is an excellent high school player, not just a college prospect. Vito Rocca, another player headed to the Ivy League (Dartmouth), leads Evanston, one of the state’s best teams, without much fanfare.</p><p><b>12. Which teams were overlooked in the preseason Super 25?</b></p><p>Young, Lyons, Moline, Crystal Lake South, Rock Island, Marshall and Rich just missed the rankings. Mount Carmel (missing football players early) and New Trier (injuries) would have cracked the rankings in other circumstances.</p><p><b>13. What is the must-see game of the year?</b></p><p>Bolingbrook vs. Neuqua Valley in the When Sides Collide shootout at Benet. Pettigrew and Kelly, the state’s biggest stars, will meet up on Jan. 23. The teams split two games last season.</p><p><b>14. What is the strongest conference in the area?</b></p><p>The Catholic League Blue is loaded. St. Ignatius, DePaul Prep, Marist, Benet and St. Laurence are ranked. Mount Carmel, Brother Rice and St. Patrick are just outside the Super 25, and Loyola is always strong.</p><p><b>15. Which sophomores will emerge as stars?</b></p><p>There are several candidates. The top tier includes Mount Carmel’s Ronald Johnson, King’s DK Heard, Bloomington’s Dallas Marshall, Denym Wallace of New Trier, De La Salle’s Zahari Threatt and Emurion Jackson of East St. Louis. Keep an eye on Leo big man Elon Henderson, Young’s TJ Jamison and St. Laurence guard Evan Lemons.</p><p><b>16. Who are the area’s best big men?</b></p><p>The list is not long. Alex Sirbu, a 6-9 senior at Buffalo Grove, and 6-9 Amari Williams of Shepard lead the list. Other 6-9 or taller players with potential include Oswego’s Cole Janson and Mount Carmel's Tim Adenrele.</p><p><b>17. What’s going on with Romeoville?</b></p><p>Several talented players transferred to Romeoville, which returns senior guard Jamarri Fears, the younger brother of Jeremy and Jeremiah Fears. The Spartans could be a top-15 or even top-10 team this season, depending on who is ruled eligible.</p><p><b>18. Who are the new coaches to watch?</b></p><p>Former West Aurora and Kaneland coach Brian Johnson takes over at Oswego East after Ryan Velasquez’s very successful nine-year run. Veteran Al Biancalana is now in charge at St. Viator, and Garrett Gatz is the new head coach at Schaumburg.</p><p><b>19. What’s the most interesting development?</b></p><p>The 35-second shot clock has finally arrived. Most high-profile events used it over the past two seasons, but it will now feature in every game, including the state playoffs.</p><p><b>20. Which star players transferred away?</b></p><p>Jaxson Davis, Quinton Kitt, Jeffrey Hassan and KJ Miller left the state for prep schools.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-430000" name="html-embed-module-430000"></a><iframe title="No Shot Clock, Ep. 207: Revealing the 2026-27 statewide preseason Super 25 rankings" allowtransparency="true" height="150" width="100%" style="border: none; min-width: min(100%, 430px);height:150px;" scrolling="no" data-name="pb-iframe-player" src="https://www.podbean.com/player-v2/?i=u6iwm-1bb41bc-pb&from=pb6admin&share=1&download=1&rtl=0&fonts=Arial&skin=1&font-color=auto&logo_link=episode_page&btn-skin=c73a3a" loading="lazy"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: 'Saturday Night Live' sketch touches raw caregiver nerve
entries.summary: <p>Did you see "Sister," the Saturday Night Live sketch? If not, give yourself a cookie for not spending your life on the internet. Because "Sister" owned all forms of social media this week, as every person traded it with every other person. You should watch it right now:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/-X9dxL17t1k?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Sister - SNL"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>If you can't, the sketch — its actual name is "Elder Care Product" — is a parody of pharmaceutical commercials.</p><p>"Dad, did you take your meds today?" says comic John Mulaney, laying a concerned hand on a white haired gent's shoulder.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1e0000" name="module-1e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>"Uh, I ... ah, well don't quite remember," the confused coot sputters. Mulaney looks earnestly into the camera.</p><p>"My dad means the world to me," he intones. "So when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible. ... I didn't know where to turn. That's when I heard about ... 'Sister.' "</p><p>Big laugh from the audience. He continues:</p><p>"'Sister' is a live-in, 24-hour elder care provider that is completely free — and also your sister. Now I don't have to worry about dad getting the care and attention he needs because I can get back to <i>my</i> life and the stuff <i>I</i> like to do."</p><p>The sketch touches a raw nerve of American life. Up to 50 million Americans are unpaid caregivers for relatives, and two-thirds of those are women. </p><p>Shucking obligations to your aged parents is an American folk ailment. I know a woman who went bankrupt and had to sell her home to support her ailing parents while her siblings refused to help.</p><p>I immediately messaged a link to the sketch to a friend, whose relationship with her brothers was shattered because of how they ignored their parents.</p><p>"You saw this?" I wrote.</p><p>"My daughter sent me the link," she said. "I couldn't believe that sketch. It's really pretty breathtaking. So perfect on every level. Once I got it, I sent it to all my female friends, sending this to everybody but my brothers. It's too bad I don't speak to them, so I could send them this."</p><p>I've watched this particular family tragedy play out over a decade, and so summarizing it feels like saying, "Then World War II occurred." But this friend — who didn't want to be identified because of the personal nature of all this — and many others have to handle the endless logistics of caring for declining parents while siblings or other relatives shrugged and said, in essence, "Not our table."</p><p>In "Sister," a doctor in a white coat comes on and explains, "Years of internalized sexism warp Sister's brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility and somehow not yours." </p><p>I've seen that in action — I know a guy who wouldn't see his mother with Alzheimer's because she wouldn't remember the visit, so why bother? My friend answered that.</p><p>"She does need human contact," she said. </p><p>My father has dementia, and here I should put in a plug for the men. Two-thirds of caregivers being women means one-third are male, and with our own sister being in Dallas, managing care for our dad falls to my brother and myself. Kudos to him because he really stepped up. I could not do it without him, and like to think he could not do it without me. And yes, we both know we're lucky: We only need to handle the logistics. Many must also must do the hands-on care, a far greater challenge.</p><p>Comedy can snap a spotlight on a truth sitting in plain sight, ignored, for years.</p><p>So watch "Sister," and ask yourself: Am I the sister? Or the brother?</p><p>"I didn't cry after watching it," my friend said. "But I wanted to."</p><p>You can't pretend that a three-minute comedy sketch will change the world. People have a genius for rationalizing whatever it is they want to do.</p><p>I've come up with five good reasons to visit my father, even though he doesn't always know I'm there, never mind that I've been there: 1) the need to check that he's being cared for, to let the staff know this isn't some forgotten sack of meat, but a loved person; 2) sometimes he seems to enjoy the visit; 3) it's the right thing to do; 4) if it were me, I'd want my boys to visit, even if I didn't know they were there; 5) I'm modeling behavior for those kids who, when my turn comes, might remember that I didn't turn my back on my parents.</p><p>That last reason is why I don't worry too much about whether my friend's brothers saw "Sister." Karma is a wheel, and they will grow old just like their parents. Payback may be coming.</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams has top-selling jersey on Fanatics for first half of NFL season
entries.summary: <p>Even with an injury keeping him out three games, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams’ jersey was the leading seller on Fanatics in the first half of the season.</p><p>Williams outdid former MVP Josh Allen of the Bills and Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba for the top spot. Packers quarterback Jordan Love was fourth, followed by likely future Hall of Famer Fred Warner of the 49ers.</p><p>There are many Williams No. 18 jerseys on Fanatics website, including all three the Bears plan to wear this season: home navy, road white and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/11/bears-packers-rivalries-uniform-christmas-day-nike-alternate-soldier-field" >the throwback-inspired rivalry jersey for Christmas Day against the Packers</a>. They also sell ones from previous seasons, like the orange alternate and other throwbacks.</p><p>Fanatics is the NFL’s retail partner, and jerseys sold on other platforms aren’t counted in their totals.</p><p>Williams went into the season as one of the hottest names in football, so much so that Jaguars coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/31/bears-coach-ben-johnson-on-jaguars-liam-coens-shot-at-qb-caleb-williams-he-can-handle-it" >Liam Coen complained about it</a>, and was on the cover of the Madden video game.</p><p>He had a big game in the opener, then hurt his hamstring against the Vikings and missed the next three. When he returned, he played the best three-game stretch of his career and vaulted himself into the MVP race.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Late Bears matriarch Virginia McCaskey beaten out for Hall nod
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> matriarch Virginia McCaskey won’t make it to the Pro Football Hall of Fame this year.</p><p>One of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/04/bears-virginia-mccaskey-advances-pro-hall-of-fame-vote-contributor-finalist-nfl" target="_blank" >five finalists</a> for the Hall’s contributor nomination, McCaskey lost out to Patriots owner Robert Kraft. The subcommittee will present him to the Hall for general inclusion, which he’s likely to receive.</p><p>He’ll likely enter alongside former Patriots head coach Bill Belichick, who was nomination by the coaching subcommittee. Belichick and Kraft worked together from 2000-23.</p><p>At least 80% of the Hall’s full selection committee must vote to allow them in early next year. The winners — chosen from 13 players and the two subcommittee picks — will be announced at NFL Honors during Super Bowl week. Enshrinement will take place in August in Canton, Ohio.</p><p>Kraft beat out former executive John Wooten, who ran the Fritz Pollard Alliance, which worked to advance diversity of coaches and executives; former Washington player Doug Williams, the first Black quarterback to win the Super Bowl; former Canton Bulldogs owner Ralph Hay; and McCaskey, who died last year at age 102.</p>

entries.title: Grand Theft Auto VI release turned into real-life workout at Roscoe Village gym
entries.summary: <p>Wolfgang Weidler had been counting down to the release of Grand Theft Auto VI for months. By Thursday morning, he'd already spent an hour playing the highly anticipated video game before heading to work at Crosstown Fitness in Roscoe Village, where he’s a trainer.</p><p>He was so engrossed, he said, that he lost track of time.</p><p>“Oh, my gosh – it is so immersive,” Weidler said. “You can literally talk to any non-playable character … you literally get sucked in.”</p><p>The latest installment in the hugely popular Grand Theft Auto franchise, GTA VI has already generated an estimated $1.84 billion in revenue as of release day, based on sales of about 19 million copies, according to market research firm Sensor Tower. The game is the first new main installment in the series in 13 years.</p><p>But Weidler, 22, didn't want to simply celebrate the game's release at home. He brought its fictional, Miami-inspired setting of Vice City to the gym, transforming three classes scheduled for 10 a.m., noon and 4:30 p.m. Thursday into a GTA VI experience.</p><p>The setup included six workout stations with exercise names like “Run From The Cops” and “Break Open The Vault,” inflatable palm trees, photoshopped graphics of gym staff members reimagined as video game characters and a playlist Weidler mixed himself, full of Latin tunes and Miami-inspired beats.</p><p>Weidler said he spent about 15 hours planning the classes, including marketing the event through a entries.title: DT Jeffery Simmons gets 'deep breath,' settles into new life as star of Bears' defense
entries.summary: <p>New defensive tackle <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/03/el-jefe-takes-charge-dt-jeffery-simmons-embraces-role-responsibility-as-new-boss-of-bears-defense" target="_blank" >Jeffery Simmons</a> was a revolutionary force for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ defense in his first two games and he hadn’t even fully settled in. Imagine what he’ll do now that he’s much more comfortable.</p><p>Simmons spent the bye week back in Nashville, the city he abruptly left last month when the Bears traded two first-round picks to the Titans for him, and immersed himself in everything from the playbook to coach Ben Johnson’s “Good, better, best” chant that he stumbled through when he first arrived.</p><p>“I was able to just take a deep breath finally,” Simmons said Thursday after practice.</p><p>The Oct. 29 trade jolted him just four months after signing a massive contract extension to stay with the Titans through 2030. He was at their facility working out early in the morning when his agent Todd France called with the news, and by the end of the day he was at Halas Hall.</p><p>Simmons said in an appearance on <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fc6oLeQ7FVs" target="_blank" >The Rich Eisen Show</a> he was “pissed” because the trade blindsided him. He’d seen plenty of trades over the years, but never thought it’d be him given how well he’d established himself with the Titans. He pointed to his great relationship with owner Amy Adams Strunk and believed himself to be “the glue trying to hold everything together in Tennessee.”</p><p>Amid that whirlwind, he did his best to jump into the flow with a new team. He was an instant hit with a sack in each of his first two games with the Bears, but saw quite a bit to correct once he did a deeper dive into defensive coordinator Dennis Allen’s playbook.</p><p>“Making sure everything is cleaner,” Simmons said. “Some of the stuff that I played the last game, I wasn't 100% [right]. I [also] did a lot of self-scouting of not just here, but even with my seven games in Tennessee. What can I get better?</p><p>“That's what I did over the bye week, especially towards the end, but early in that week, I just set my tail down and took a deep breath, did a little packing and enjoyed family time."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="zxx" dir="ltr"><a href="https://t.co/ep4KLsNTMI">pic.twitter.com/ep4KLsNTMI</a></p>— Patrick Finley (@patrickfinley) <a href="https://x.com/patrickfinley/status/2123512986853613788?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 19, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Him winging it was pretty impressive nonetheless and sparked fellow defensive linemen Grady Jarrett and Montez Sweat because of the attention he drew. And now that the Bears can get pressure without blitzing, it opens up all kinds of wrinkles for Allen, who called it “a fun problem to have.”</p><p>Simmons’ transition to the Bears was eased by their enthusiastic embrace and the pursuit of a championship — he’s playing on “a brighter stage,” he said. He hasn’t been to the playoffs since 2022, and the Titans were 1-6 when they dealt him.</p><p>He was blown away by the crowd’s roar at Soldier Field when he was introduced before his home debut, saying the fans “accepted me before I even touchdown down in town” and calling it “amazing to see.” It’s been like that in the locker room, too.</p><p>Simmons missed time this week with what the team listed as a knee injury, though it might’ve been more of a load management strategy with the Bears about to host the Saints on Sunday and visit the Lions on Thanksgiving. He said he felt “fine” after limited work Thursday.</p><p>“Ninety-nine problems, but this ain't one,” Simmons said, referring to his jersey number and Jay-Z’s 2004 hit. “I'll be out there Sunday."</p>

entries.title: Did you take the day off to play GTA VI? Tell us all about it.
entries.summary: <p>The long-awaited and much-hyped Grand Theft Auto VI finally saw release on Thursday, promising a long weekend of play for fans of the series — and, for many, a steep drop in productivity. </p><p>Easily one of the biggest games on the planet, reportedly reaching 20 million pre-orders before launch, the game follows two lovers embarking on a life of crime in the fictional Vice City. Some took to social media to announce their plans to take the day off from work or school to spend as much time as possible in the game's world.</p><p>The Sun-Times wants to hear from you.</p><p>Did you make plans to stay home to play GTA? Are you enjoying it so far? Do you plan on staying in the whole weekend?</p><p>Please fill out the following form. entries.title: What factors could influence Connor Bedard's surgery vs. rehab decision for shoulder injury?
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> star Connor Bedard's next step — after suffering another <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/18/blackhawks-connor-bedard-shoulder-injury" >injury</a> to his right shoulder — is deciding whether or not to undergo surgery.</p><p>"Collectively, as a group, I would say we’re still gathering information, weighing the different decision processes between rehab and surgery," coach Jeff Blashill said Thursday.</p><p>Blashill ruled out Bedard for the Hawks' upcoming three-game road trip against the Flames, Canucks and Kraken, but it's clear the 21-year-old forward will miss considerably more time than that.</p><p>The question is how much more time. Last December, when he injured his right shoulder and opted for a rehab-only recovery process, he was cleared to return after four weeks. </p><p>In July, when he injured his left shoulder and opted for surgery, he was cleared after three months. Both of those timelines were faster than initially estimated.</p><p>Bedard's agent, Don Meehan, said in July that Dr. Peter Millett, the Colorado-based surgeon who operated on Bedard's left shoulder, recommended surgery in that instance because he determined the left shoulder had suffered more damage than the right previously had.</p><p>It's unknown how much damage the right shoulder suffered from this new injury; that's presumably what Bedard is currently determining.</p><p>But in July, Bedard knew most of the three-to-four-month recovery time would fall during the offseason, costing him only a small portion of the regular season.</p><p>In this case, that same timeline would knock him out until February or March, costing him most of the rest of the season. That could motivate him to consider at least putting off surgery until after the April 10 season finale.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.jorgechahlamd.com/" target="_blank" >Dr. Jorge Chahla</a>, a sports medicine surgeon at Midwest Orthopaedics at Rush, explained Thursday that several factors influence the surgery vs. rehab decision after a shoulder injury.</p><p>One is which direction the shoulder is dislocating (to the front is most common). Another is the size of the tear in the labrum, a ring of fibrocartilage that lines the shoulder socket.</p><p>Then a third and perhaps most important factor is bone loss from the socket itself.</p><p>"Bone loss is what actually makes these tears more dangerous," Chahla said. "The socket is kind of a like a pear: bigger on the bottom, thinner on the top. As soon as you start losing some bone, which usually happens with multiple dislocation episodes, you start to have bigger issues with dislocating with less force."</p><p>Once as little as 13.5% of the socket has been lost — and especially once 20% has been lost — patients can suffer permanent reductions in range of motion, strength or functionality. For a pro athlete like Bedard, that would be a particularly major problem.</p><p>It typically takes multiple dislocations, not just one, to reach the 13.5% bone-loss threshold, Chahla said. But every subsequent dislocation has a chance of causing more damage.</p><p>Chahla referenced a 2017 <a class="Link" href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28657778/" target="_blank" >study</a> by Jonathan Dickens in the American Journal of Sports Medicine that found 90% of collegiate athletes who underwent shoulder surgeries returned to play without recurrence of the injury, whereas 40% of athletes who only underwent rehab returned to play without recurrence.</p><p>However, 40% isn't nothing. For many other types of injuries, that percentage would be much lower.</p><p>"It's a decision as to whether he wants to face some time off now vs. delaying it, playing the recovery card and seeing how far he can go," Chahla said. "Sometimes, athletes can get lucky."</p><p>That same 2017 study also found athletes who underwent surgery before their next season were nearly six times more likely to complete that next season without recurrent shoulder instability. </p><p>That finding is relevant to Bedard's already surgically repaired left shoulder, and it would presumably be something for him to consider come April regarding his right shoulder.</p><p>Still, Chahla clarified that even a surgically repaired shoulder isn't as strong as a normal, never-dislocated shoulder. The risks increase no matter what.</p>

entries.title: State regulators slash Peoples Gas rate hike by more than $103 million
entries.summary: <p>State regulators on Thursday slashed nearly $104 million from a rate hike requested by Peoples Gas, meaning Chicago residents will see a slimmer increase to their heating bills in the new year.</p><p>The decision handed down by the Illinois Commerce Commission also keeps up the pressure on the Chicago utility to wrap up its long-running pipeline replacement efforts within the next decade, while Peoples Gas warned the order will prevent them from completing some “critical day-to-day safety work.”</p><p>“The ICC’s responsibility is to balance the interests of Illinois’ utilities and their consumers, and the increase approved today reflects a fair and reasonable determination reached over the course of an 11-month legal proceeding,” ICC chairman Doug Scott said in a statement.</p><p>In January, Peoples Gas requested a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2026/01/05/peoples-gas-rate-hike-chicago-heating-bills" target="_blank" ><u>$202 million hike</u></a> that consumer advocates and Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/05/06/illinois-attorney-general-kwame-raoul-rate-cut-request-peoples-gas-202m-hike-proposal" target="_blank" ><u>blasted</u></a> as an “unsupported and unexplained” cost increase.</p><p>The utility lowered its request to $144 million over the summer, before ICC administrative law judges <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2026/10/08/peoples-gas-rate-hike-icc-regulatory-judges-recommendation" target="_blank" ><u>recommended</u></a> the state panel slash that figure to $66 million.</p><p>The five-person commission, which has tightened the leash on Peoples Gas in its rate cases over the past few years, cut even further down to the roughly $40 million hike approved Thursday.</p><p>It wasn’t immediately clear what impact that’ll have on Chicago heating bills come January. A $144 million hike would’ve tacked up to $8 more onto the average monthly residential bill.</p><p>While the approved total is less than a fifth of what Peoples Gas initially requested, the ICC still expects the utility to meet the 2035 deadline previously set by the state to replace hundreds of miles of aging, subterranean gas lines across the city.</p><p>That work started about 15 years ago, running many years behind schedule and billions of dollars over budget.</p><p>But Peoples Gas says the new order could halt important work, as it has argued for years in seeking the state’s approval to charge residents more money. The ICC granted the utility a record-high $306 million hike in 2023.</p><p>“We understand the commission today approved our continued pipe retirement plans, however today’s decision to cut $25 million in critical day-to-day safety work is surprising and extremely disappointing,” a Peoples Gas spokesperson said in an email. “We must review the final order but based on the ICC’s verbal discussion, this decision ignores the recommendations of their expert staff and administrative law judges regarding this needed work.”</p><p>Consumer advocates weren’t happy with the pipeline decision either, arguing the state should clamp down further.</p><p>“We commend the commission for significantly lowering this rate hike, but we’re disappointed they did not end the failing Peoples Gas pipe replacement program,” Abe Scarr, director of the Illinois Public Interest Research Group, said in a statement. “Until the commission ends this pipe replacement program, wasteful Peoples Gas spending will burden Chicagoans with harmful pollution and excessive rate hikes.”</p><p>Sarah Moskowitz, executive director of the Citizens Utility Board, commended the ICC for reining in Peoples Gas’ 10.10% requested return on equity down to 9.48%.</p><p>“The utility’s profit quest on the backs of struggling Chicagoans was especially brazen given that Peoples has recorded record earnings in seven of the last nine years,” Moskowitz said in a statement. “We hope today’s decision by the ICC is a harbinger of even stricter limits on Peoples Gas in the future.”</p><p>Residents struggling to pay their bills are encouraged to visit <a class="Link" href="http://icc.illinois.gov/consumers/utility-energy-assistance" target="_blank" ><u>icc.illinois.gov/consumers/utility-energy-assistance</u></a>, or call 1-833-711-0374.</p>

entries.title: As the Muslim population grows swiftly in the US, a Berwyn mosque is flourishing
entries.summary: <p>For years, Latino converts to Islam in the Chicago area struggled to find religious spaces and support networks that reflected both their faith and their cultural backgrounds.</p><p>That includes Raul Gonzalez, who grew up Pentecostal in Humboldt Park and converted to Islam 26 years ago. </p><p>“Islam talks about the unity of the believers, and so I was looking for more brothers, more people like myself, Latino Muslim converts,” he said. </p><p>Then he met Christopher AbdulKareem Pavlicek, who felt the same way, and they started looking for a space where Spanish-speaking Muslims could gather.</p><p>They found it in a shuttered church in Berwyn.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure
