class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Imam Christopher AbdulKarim Pavlícek stands with his wife Karen Rios, who was born in Mexico, and their 4-month-old daughter in the Ojala Islamic Center at 1900 S. Oak Park Ave. in Berwyn.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In February, on the first day of Ramadan, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2026/03/05/latino-muslims-ojala-islamic-center" target="_blank" >Ojala Islamic Center opened in Berwyn as the Midwest’s first Latino-led mosque</a>, offering converts a place to practice Islam while maintaining ties to their cultural heritage. Pavlicek is its founder and serves as imam.</p><p>“I was searching for a community for a long time,” Pavlicek said. “Nobody's doing it. I have to do it myself."</p><p>The mosque opened amid a shifting religious landscape. <a class="Link" href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2026/11/18/the-future-of-world-religions-population-growth-projections-2020-2070/" target="_blank" >New Pew Research Center projections</a> released Wednesday show the Muslim population in North America is expected to more than triple, from about 6 million people in 2020 to 20 million by 2070. In the United States, the Muslim population is projected to grow by about 9 million, reaching roughly 4% of the country's population — outpacing Christianity's growth. </p><p>Although the Christian population is expected to continue growing, Muslims and religiously unaffiliated people are projected to grow faster.</p><p>Those shifts could reshape the religious makeup of a city like Chicago, where Christianity has historically dominated, said Dr. Emily Crews, executive director of the Martin Marty Center for the Public Understanding of Religion at the University of Chicago's Divinity School and a scholar of American religions.</p><p>“100 years ago, Chicago was 90-plus percent Christian,” Crews said. “100 years later, we're looking at where Chicago still has a Christian majority, but that number is shrinking.”</p><p>“The Christian majority is shaping the culture less and less, which I think makes for a really interesting diversity of congregations,” she added.</p><p>Illinois has the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/race-class-communities/2022/07/28/illinois-has-the-most-muslims-per-capita-in-the-us " target="_blank" >nation’s highest concentration of Muslims per capita</a>, according to a 2022 study by the Institute for Social Policy and Understanding and the University of Illinois Chicago. More than 350,000 Illinoisans identify as Muslim, mostly residing in the Chicago area. About 8% of the state's Muslim population is Hispanic, the study found.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-6a0000" name="image-6a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7625039/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6316x3545+0+334/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F80%2F2f0f2d7c443aaad62a01503fe3f1%2Fpewmuslimgrowth-261118-01.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/578f03a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6316x3545+0+334/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F80%2F2f0f2d7c443aaad62a01503fe3f1%2Fpewmuslimgrowth-261118-01.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3b4bd89/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6316x3545+0+334/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F80%2F2f0f2d7c443aaad62a01503fe3f1%2Fpewmuslimgrowth-261118-01.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Raul Gonzalez at the Ojala Islamic Center in Berwyn. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3b4bd89/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6316x3545+0+334/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F80%2F2f0f2d7c443aaad62a01503fe3f1%2Fpewmuslimgrowth-261118-01.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c04204a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6316x3545+0+334/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F80%2F2f0f2d7c443aaad62a01503fe3f1%2Fpewmuslimgrowth-261118-01.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3b4bd89/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6316x3545+0+334/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbe%2F80%2F2f0f2d7c443aaad62a01503fe3f1%2Fpewmuslimgrowth-261118-01.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Raul Gonzalez, who is of Puerto Rican heritage, was happy to find other Latino Muslims at the Ojala Islamic Center at 1900 S. Oak Park Ave. in Berwyn, which opened earlier this year.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ahmed Rehab, executive director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations' Chicago chapter, said he's seeing the most rapid Muslim growth among young women and Latino converts.</p><p>“A lot of Muslims don't know that Latinos are the fastest-growing community,” he said. “When you learn that, they're surprised themselves.”</p><p>Pew projects that migration will drive much of Islam's expansion in North America. Muslims' higher birth rates are also contributing to growth, according to Pew research. </p><p>But immigration and birth rates tell only part of the story. At Ojala, many members were raised in other faiths before converting to Islam after coming to the United States and exploring their own spiritual identities.</p><p>Pavlicek said the congregation is as much “convert-led” as it is “Latino-led,” with much of its community made up of people from different religious and cultural backgrounds who are embracing Islam for the first time.</p><p>Crews said Muslim congregations can offer immigrants a sense of community and practical support as newcomers establish themselves.</p><p>“If you're a new migrant and you're looking for a home, literally and figuratively, a place where you can feel like you belong, but also where not just your spiritual needs, but your physical or material needs are met, Muslim congregations in Chicago are incredibly civically oriented,” she said.</p><p>Nelson Julio-Polanco, born in the Dominican Republic and raised Catholic, found a sense of belonging at Ojala, which offers services in Arabic, English and Spanish. As the only Muslim in his family, Julio-Polanco said speaking Spanish with other Muslims made the community especially welcoming.</p><p>“When they founded this organization, I felt like, wow, I can speak Spanish to these people and they're Muslims too,” he said. “We have the same culture.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Oak Park Ave. in Berwyn.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>After four years as a practicing Muslim, Julio-Polanco is making the pilgrimage to Mecca for the first time Friday.</p><p>Ojala's growth comes in a city where Catholicism remains deeply woven into the cultural identity of many Berwyn neighborhoods, particularly Latino communities. The Catholic Church is also seeing growth: 1,059 adults became Catholic in Chicago during this year's Easter season, a 52% increase from the previous year, according to the Archdiocese of Chicago.</p><p>But Crews said the increase, while statistically significant, doesn't reflect the broader trajectory of Christianity in the United States.</p><p>“I think any sort of triumphal narrative that says like, 'Ah, we're all back on track and look, Christianity is going to regain its national dominance,'… it's unrealistic,” she said.</p><p>While some younger Americans, particularly white men, are converting to Orthodox Christianity and Catholicism, Crews said Pew's projections underscore a broader trend: People are leaving Christianity at a faster rate than they are leaving Islam.</p><p>For Pavlicek, Ojala is "filling a void" for people of faith in the area. </p><p>The building at 1900 S. Oak Park Ave. served as First Reformed Church of Berwyn <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagohistory.org/ojala-foundation-and-making-space-for-chicagolands-latino-muslim-communities/" target="_blank" >for 77 years,</a> according to the Chicago History Museum.</p><p>The transition reflects a practical convergence, Rehab said. Some churches with shrinking congregations are selling and looking to sell their buildings, while a growing Muslim population needs space. </p><p>“You have a growing population in a historically religiously diverse city, you have growing migrant populations, but you don't have the community spaces to serve them,” Crews said.</p><p>Like Pavlicek, Rehab sees the mosque as part of Chicago's religious history, rather than a departure from it.</p><p>“It's sort of a win-win on both ends,” Rehab said. “Muslims appreciate and even embrace the Catholic legacy of Chicago, which lives on. We're contributing our own touch to the painting.”</p><p>In Berwyn, Pavlicek said worshippers like himself travel long distances to attend Ojala, the only mosque within a six-mile radius. As the congregation grows, he said, Ojala already is looking to establish another Islamic center in Pilsen to serve more Chicagoans.</p><p>Karen Rios, Pavlicek's wife and mother of their two children, said the mosque is where her religious and cultural identities can coexist. Raised Catholic in Mexico City, she came to Chicago to study to become an au pair. But she decided to stay, she said, to practice her Muslim faith freely in her community.</p><p>“I wanted to pray almost every day here, like to stay with the community, so that's why it was also part of my choice to stay here,” she said. “To practice my religion.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: White Sox banking on Dustin May's untapped upside, and still hunting for more additions
entries.summary: <p>As <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> general manager Chris Getz led right-hander Dustin May into Rate Field’s conference and learning center to announce his three-year, $52.5 million contract, the back wall was lined with team staffers who would only be familiar if you flipped the media guide to the page listing data engineers and research analysts.</p><p>That and bullpen catcher Bennett Markinson, a data science and economics double major from Northwestern. In other words, people who know May’s pitch metrics outstrip his 4.70 ERA from 2026, and would view that figure as a crude way to assess a pitcher.</p><p>And not a predictive one.</p><p>“He has his best years ahead of him,” Getz declared. It’s not a typical comment to pair with lauding May’s four World Series rings, but it was a shared sentiment.</p><p>“My first five seasons, it was very minimal usage,” said May. “To have the last two basically full years, I feel like those were my first two full years in the big leagues. I was honestly still learning and figuring myself out.”</p><p>Despite the emphasis on untapping the upside that May’s 97 mph fastball, 6-foot-6 frame and past prospect rankings suggest, the 29-year-old had become a bit of a white whale for Getz. He confessed to unsuccessfully pursuing May last offseason, and this August at the trade deadline.</p><p>“He didn’t have a whole lot to say in the matter at the deadline, to my knowledge,” Getz quipped.</p><p>For his part, May insisted the persistence wasn’t in vain. After raising his arm slot in 2026 and throwing a cutter more to tamp down the damage lefty hitters have inflicted on him over his career, May indicated the White Sox proposed similar ideas in free-agent conversations last winter, and that he wasn’t shocked by the club’s leap to the postseason.</p><p>“I was very close last year, but I think there’s some more untapped things that I could work on,” May said.</p><p>Seemingly more progress is needed after May yielded eight homers in 47⅔ innings with the Brewers after being dealt from the Cardinals in August, but the Sox aren’t alone in buying that his avoidance of the injured list this year is further evidence he’s on the right track. Other teams have analysts parsing stuff metrics to hunt upside plays too, and many could fill up more rows of a conference room than the Sox.</p><p>A source told the Sun-Times that half the league made inquiries on May at one point, before the field winnowed to a half dozen serious suitors, with the Sox’ winning bid edging three other clubs at the end. As a development project, May spins the baseball like few can, was healthy enough to make 33 starts this year, is ready to “party in the dugout” with his rambunctious new teammates, and was a compelling target to teams — like the White Sox — seeking to identify frontline starters while paying a rate comfortably under what frontline results would demand.</p><p>As a solution to the White Sox only having one usable starting pitcher last month, May would look better as part of a multi-prong strategy. Getz affirmed the club is still prowling the starting pitching waters, and he expects to have another addition to tout before the league shuts down late on the night of Dec. 1.</p><p>“When this press conference is finished, we are going to continue to get on the phone,” Getz said. “We are very specific in our targets and we know what our needs are and we are going to try to get as much done as we can.”</p><p>That’s not going to conclude with the Sox having a fully hashed-out pitching hierarchy two weeks from now, and certainly not with a proven Grant Taylor replacement in place with the bullpen. For now they’re just adding, and it will get figured out later.</p><p>“We created the expectation around here that we're going to do whatever we can to win games,” said manager Will Venable. “It starts with getting as many players that you think can help you do that.”</p>

entries.title: Reckless homicide, DUI charges for motorist in Bishop Ford double fatal wreck in Pullman in February
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago motorist was drunk and acting recklessly when she slammed into a light post, leaving two of her passengers dead in February on the Bishop Ford Freeway in Pullman, Illinois State Police said. </p><p>Alisia A. Agnew, 25, was allegedly under the influence when she was driving a Chevrolet truck on Feb.19 that left the roadway, struck a light post, and rolled over on the 111th Street ramp to I-94, according to Illinois State Police. </p><p>The crash caused three people to be ejected from the truck. Troopers gave CPR to Lazarus Gonzales, 23, and Boaz Flemister, 17, but they died at the scene, state police and the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>Both Chicagoans, Gonzales was of the city's Douglas neighborhood and Flemister was of the Calumet Heights neighborhood, according to the medical examiner's office. </p><p>Agnew and two other passengers were taken to nearby hospitals, state police said. </p><p>On Wednesday, Agnew was charged with two counts of reckless homicide, two counts of aggravated driving under the influence involving death, and one count of aggravated driving under the influence causing great bodily harm. <br></p>

entries.summary: <p>Six Chicago restaurants have been newly added to the Michelin Guide, the company <a class="Link" href="https://guide.michelin.com/us/en/article/travel/new-michelin-restaurants-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>announced</u></a> Wednesday.</p><p>Additions include <a class="Link" href="https://www.allwellchicago.com/" target="_blank" ><u>All Well</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.petiteedith.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Petite Edith</u></a>, two casual concepts from chef-teams that have previously earned stars for fine dining destinations, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.oldfriendchicago.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Lao Peng You</u></a>, a favorite local<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/food-drink/2026/01/13/chicago-soup-near-me-restaurant-carryout" target="_blank" ><u> soup spot. </u></a></p><p>Every year, French tire company Michelin produces a guide of the best restaurants and hotels across major U.S. cities. The company’s anonymous inspectors drive to hundreds of the trendiest and most popular restaurants in America, and then rank them in a system of one to three stars (the more, the better), to let the public know which ones are worth the trip.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b80000" You</u></a> is an increasingly popular Chinese restaurant with a cult following, including for its soups. Known for its traditional and flavorful dumpling and noodle dishes, the restaurant’s menu includes plenty of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2026/01/13/chicago-soup-near-me-restaurant-carryout" target="_blank" ><u>hot and cold noodles</u></a>, hearty soup dumplings and made-to-order breads. Opened by brothers Eric and Daniel Wat, the family restaurant bears a name that means “old friends” in Mandarin.</p><p>Seafood is in the spotlight at <a class="Link" href="https://www.marielachicago.com/" target="_blank" >Mariela</a>, the restaurant inside the Staypineapple Hotel in the historic Reliance Building at 1 W. Washington St. Known for its tom yum aguachile, oysters, and cocktail bar, the Downtown establishment draws inspiration from the shores of Spain, France, Southeast Asia and the Americas.</p><p>Also making the list for the first time is <a class="Link" href="https://www.midosujichicago.com/" target="_blank" >Midōsuji</a>, inside the Chicago Athletic Association, an à la carte hand roll bar with only eight seats. It serves fatty tuna and wasabi rolls, paired with cocktails, beers and sake.</p><p>Another restaurant added to the guide is <a class="Link" href="https://www.atsumerurestaurant.com/" target="_blank" >Atsumeru</a> in the Noble Square neighborhood, where chef Devin Denzer is blending Japanese and Nordic cuisine. entries.title: Mujer de Chicago es condenada a cárcel tras llamar a la policía con denuncia falsa a un jaripeo en los suburbios
entries.summary: <p>Una activista por los derechos de los animales en Chicago fue sentenciada a 60 días de cárcel, 60 horas de servicio comunitario y un año de libertad condicional tras ser declarada culpable de hostigar a despachadores en el interior del estado y de hacer una denuncia falsa de un tiroteo con la intención de que la policía acudiera a un jaripeo donde ella creía que se maltrataba ganado.</p><p>La residente del lado norte, Jodie Wiederkehr, de 57 años, fue sentenciada este mes por el juez Anthony Peska de la Corte del Condado de Ogle, después de que un jurado la declarara culpable de un delito grave y un delito menor. Con crédito por buen comportamiento, la condena de 60 días se reduciría a 30 días.</p><p>En los últimos años se han celebrado rodeos en patios traseros en localidades rurales y semi-rurales de Illinois, incluyendo algunos sitios suburbanos.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e70000" name="module-e70000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los jaripeos suelen incluir un evento llamado coleadero, que consiste en que alguien a caballo persigue a un novillo que huye y le enrosca una pierna alrededor de la cola con la intención de hacerlo caer. Además de las lesiones por la caída, a veces los novillos se quedan con la cola arrancada en el proceso, algo conocido en inglés como "degloving".</p><p>Los activistas por los derechos de los animales han tratado de detener esta práctica, argumentando que viola la ley estatal contra el maltrato animal, aunque algunos dicen que la ley es demasiado vaga para enjuiciar. Ha habido intentos legislativos fallidos para precisar la ley y prohibir explícitamente el "steer tailing" en todo el estado, mientras que algunos gobiernos de condado también están actuando al respecto.</p><p>Wiederkehr —miembro de SHARK, siglas en inglés de SHowing Animals Respect and Kindness— dijo que estaba monitoreando a distancia uno de los jaripeos celebrados el año pasado en el área de Rochelle, al oeste de DeKalb, “recibiendo las anotaciones en vivo del equipo de campo que estaba allí” monitoreando el evento mediante un dron.</p><p>“Se estaban desollando novillos, se les exigía en exceso, se les abusaba criminalmente”, dijo.</p><p>Dijo que llamó numerosas veces al número no urgente del Sheriff del Condado de Ogle y, frustrada y enfadada porque nadie iba a ser enviado, finalmente le dijo a una despachadora que había un tiroteo en un intento por forzar una respuesta policial.</p><p>No había habido ningún tiroteo, y Wiederkehr dijo que lamenta haberlo dicho y que se siente avergonzada, pero que en el momento estaba “angustiada”.</p><p>“En un rodeo anterior allí se les rompieron las patas a dos novillos y a un caballo”, alegó.</p><p>Insistió en que “no acosé” a los despachadores, afirmando que “cada vez que llamaba había un delito ocurriendo” que equivalía a maltrato animal, pero que no la tomaban en serio.</p><p>Sus abogados pidieron que no cumpliera pena de cárcel.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-734b40" name="image-734b40"></a> <picture class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Peska dijo en la corte que, tras leer cartas de carácter sobre Wiederkehr, está claro que se la considera “un miembro apreciado de la familia, amiga, defensora”, según una transcripción.</p><p>Aun así, dijo que es importante imponer una condena que sirva como disuasión.</p><p>“Creo que es de importancia crítica darse cuenta de que no estamos en un condado con recursos ilimitados", dijo Peska, “cuando llamas al departamento del sheriff del condado de Ogle, pueden tener dos alguaciles de servicio para todo el condado”, por lo que una llamada falsa puede apartarlos de una emergencia legítima.</p><p>Wiederkehr sostuvo que, aunque cometió un error, la oficina del sheriff realmente no creyó que hubiera habido un tiroteo, y que fue procesada porque el fiscal del condado de Ogle, Mike Rock, estaba enfadado porque Wiederkehr lo había criticado anteriormente por la falta de enjuiciamientos relacionados con los jaripeos.</p><p>Los abogados de Wiederkehr presentaron documentos en la corte describiendo esto como una “persecución procesal vengativa”.</p><p>El juez rechazó ese argumento, y Rock dijo que no es cierto.</p><p>“Nuestra fiscalía, en cada caso, busca la justicia, y eso es lo que se hizo aquí", dijo Rock. “No fue tratada peor ni mejor por quien era… cometió un acto criminal y lo perseguimos”.</p><p>“Creí que la cárcel era apropiada", añadió Rock, señalando que el estatuto permitía una pena de prisión de hasta tres años por el delito grave.</p><p>Chris Carraway, uno de los abogados de Wiederkehr, dijo que Peska anteriormente ha sido más indulgente con delitos más graves, incluido un incidente en el que un adolescente amenazó con "disparar" en una escuela y recibió 24 meses de libertad condicional.</p><p>Peska no permitió que Wiederkehr presentara una defensa basada en el argumento de que “rompí la ley para prevenir un mal mayor”, según ella. Tampoco permitió que el jurado viera un video del coleadero en el que se maltrataron animales, dijo Carraway.</p><p>Rock dijo que “querían convertir esto en un juicio de una semana sobre si el 'steer tailing' es apropiado o no, cuando la cuestión era si ella hizo llamadas repetidas y finalmente un informe falso de un delito”.</p><p>Se espera una apelación de la condena, de la sentencia o de ambas.</p><p>Bajo presión, los organizadores del jaripeo del Condado de Ogle han dejado de hacer el evento.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: No prison time for man who crashed into Border Patrol vehicle during Operation Midway Blitz
entries.summary: <p>A federal judge on<b> </b>Thursday<b> </b>gave<b> </b>a sentence of time served<b> </b>to<b> </b>a Chicago area<b> </b>man<b> </b>who spent about four days<b> </b>in custody after he drove<b> </b>a<b> </b>Ford<b> </b>truck<b> </b>into a U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicle<b> </b>during Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>U.S. District Judge LaShonda<b> </b>Hunt<b> </b>handed down the sentence to Anthony<b> </b>Gonzalez<b> </b>Alvarez, who<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/13/midway-blitz-ice-border-patrol-anthony-gonzalez-alvarez" target="_blank" >pleaded guilty</a><b> </b>in<b> </b>August<b> </b>to<b> </b>forcibly interfering with CBP officers, a misdemeanor. Alvarez is one of two people<b> </b>to be convicted of a crime<b> </b>tied to the Midway Blitz deportation campaign.</p><p>During Thursday’s hearing, the judge agreed with a prosecutor who called Alvarez’s conduct “reckless and dangerous.” But<b> </b>Hunt<b> </b>acknowledged<b> </b>Alvarez already spent time behind bars, has had few issues since his arrest<b> </b>and has agreed to pay<b> </b>$1,362<b> </b>in restitution.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/13/midway-blitz-ice-border-patrol-anthony-gonzalez-alvarez" >First Midway Blitz guilty plea scaled back as defendant contests account of crash with feds</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Before learning his sentence, Alvarez told the judge, “I regret what I did. I really do. I just want to apologize and just want to move on with my life.”</p><p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago charged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >33<b> </b>known<b> </b>defendants</a><b> </b>with crimes tied to Midway Blitz. But charges against 28<b> </b>of those individuals<b> </b>have been dropped.</p><p>So far, the only other person convicted of a crime tied to the blitz is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/27/midway-blitz-ice-border-patrol-little-village-trump-bovino" target="_blank" >Hector<b> </b>Gomez</a>. He was sentenced to 30 months in prison<b> </b>after admitting to<b> </b>firing a gun near immigration agents.</p><p>Meanwhile, federal prosecutors are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/06/broadview-6-hearing-set-to-rock-chicago-federal-courthouse-but-doj-official-could-intervene" target="_blank" >under fire</a> for alleged misconduct<b> </b>in a failed case brought against a group of Midway Blitz protesters<b> </b>known as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six.”</a></p><p>Alvarez<b> </b>admitted<b> </b>in August<b> </b>that, on Oct. 3, 2025, he<b> </b>joined<b> </b>a caravan of vehicles while<b> </b>driving<b> </b>a black<b> </b>Ford truck<b> </b>in pursuit of a CBP vehicle.<b> </b>The<b> </b>driver<b> </b>of the CBP vehicle<b> </b>tried to pull away from the caravan, including by entering the wrong lane of traffic, records show.</p><p>But<b> </b>Alvarez<b> </b>followed<b> </b>in his truck and, eventually, crashed<b> </b>into the rear passenger side<b> </b>of the CBP vehicle, according to Alvarez’s plea agreement.</p><p>Alvarez<b> </b>has<b> </b>denied<b> </b>crashing<b> </b>into<b> </b>the<b> </b>CBP<b> </b>vehicle<b> </b>on purpose.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" >Tracking every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s deportation blitz</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Assistant U.S. Attorney Stephanie<b> </b>Stern<b> </b>noted that, later that afternoon, Alvarez<b> </b>visited a police station<b> </b>to report that his truck<b> </b>had been stolen<b> </b>that morning. Then, in the evening, he<b> </b>called<b> </b>911<b> </b>to tell police he’d found his truck using a tracking device.</p><p>That wasn’t Alvarez’s first brush with the law, Stern<b> </b>noted in a court filing. Alvarez<b> </b>pleaded guilty in 2017 to resisting a police officer<b> </b>in an incident that involved Alvarez<b> </b>spitting<b> </b>on an officer, Stern wrote.</p><p>Then, in 2019, he<b> </b>pleaded guilty to attempted false impersonation of a peace officer, according to the prosecutor. She wrote that he’d been accused of using<b> </b>white and blue<b> </b>flashing lights — similar to the Chicago Police Department’s — to pull other vehicles over.</p><p>Finally, Stern told the judge<b> </b>that<b> </b>Alvarez<b> </b>was convicted<b> </b>in 2021 for a false report. Alvarez<b> </b>had<b> </b>called<b> </b>911<b> </b>to report<b> </b>his daughter<b> </b>had been kidnapped, she wrote. But it turned out the<b> </b>girl<b> </b>was<b> </b>with her mother the entire time, Stern explained.</p><p>Ricardo<b> </b>Meza, Alvarez’s defense attorney, acknowledged his client’s unlawful conduct on Thursday. But he reminded the judge that few things happen in a vacuum. And Alvarez’s encounter with the CBP vehicle occurred in the midst of an aggressive deportation campaign.</p><p>“Unfortunately, during the course of that operation, a lot of people were hurt,” Meza said. He added, “some people actually lost their lives.”</p><p>That all “stoked anger”<b> </b>in Alvarez, he said, who<b> </b>“shouldn’t have been out there.”</p><p>“He is sorry for what he has done,” Meza told the judge. “He is ready to move on with his life.”</p>
